18i6r84.text: Nikkei Inc. disclosed a new data breach, the third in about a month, that exposed 1.83 million personal information records. The Japanese giant says subsets of the data contained personally identifiable information and other sensitive details, but most records contained no identifying info. The company said that 150,000 records contained at least one of the following data types: full names, email addresses, physical addresses, telephone numbers, and dates of birth. Email addresses appeared in 120,000 records. The remaining 1.68 million records contain no identifiers, the company said, and no credit card information was exposed. Nikkei Inc. is a major Japanese business news and financial information group, owner of Financial Times, the country’s largest business-focused media company. The company employs over 10,100 people and has an annual revenue of $2.5 billion (¥393.8 billion). According to a notice Nikkei published late last week, hackers used stolen credentials to access a development system within its network during the early morning hours of October 7. The unauthorized access exposed personal information the company stored in the cloud. Nikkei revoked the abused credentials and notified the Personal Information Protection Commission on October 11. The company is currently examining the scope of the breach and noted that as of October 16, it had no evidence that the accessed information was misused or leaked online. The company has also found no signs of system compromise or data tampering resulting from this incident, and has experienced no service outages. The firm said those affected will receive individual notifications. “We are working urgently to establish the extent of the damage and determine the cause, and will implement the necessary measures to strengthen security,” Nikkei stated. This is the third cybersecurity incident that Nikkei disclosed recently. Earlier this month, the company disclosed a breach that occurred in late July, when hackers compromised an employee's Google Workspace account and accessed personal information belonging to employees and business partners. In September, Nikkei announced that threat actors hijacked another employee’s Microsoft 365 account and used it to send spear-phishing emails to the firm’s staff. BleepingComputer has contacted Nikkei for more information about the latest breach, and we will update this post once we receive a response. 1hdbrk3.text: Some downloads of the Rank Math PRO WordPress plugin from the vendor’s official website carried malware that planted hidden backdoors in a supply-chain attack last week. According to the vendor, a limited number of users who downloaded version 3.0.123 of the plugin between October 15 at 20:02 UTC and October 16 at 07:12 UTC received compromised versions that could compromise their websites upon activation. “The affected plugin files contained malware that could compromise your website if the plugin was activated,” Rank Math warned. “We immediately removed the affected files and released a clean version, Rank Math PRO v3.0.124.” Users who installed and activated the trojanized version during this 11-hour window should treat their websites as compromised and follow the clean-up procedures in the advisory from the vendor. Rank Math PRO is a WordPress search engine optimization (SEO) plugin that helps websites improve visibility in search results. It is the paid version of the free variant that is active on more than 4 million websites. Sensitive material exposed An advisory from the vendor highlights that only the PRO version was compromised and the free version of Rank Math SEO from WordPress.org remained unaffected. Rank Math says that the malware establishes persistent access, communicates with ‘rank1cdn[.]com,’ and recreates hidden backdoors when someone visits the infected website. The vendor warns that users installing the compromised version of Rank Math PRO expose database credentials, API keys, and other secrets accessible to the web server. While researching the attack, BleepingComputer discovered a PHP malware sample on VirusTotal named 'cache-preloader-fff033 (1).php' that appears to be connected to the Rank Math compromise. Although this file was not mentioned in the Rank Math or Wordfence advisories, BleepingComputer found it contained the same indicators of compromise (IoCs) included in Rank Math's alert: xmmqhn' XOR obfuscation key the '_np5pvf754c' WordPress database entry the '#ms6v46' cron job marker code for creating administrator accounts using the 'wpsupport_' username prefix and '@wp-mail.net' email addresses The malware appears to act as a first-stage deployment script that creates the 'wp-includes/class-wp-cache-util.php' backdoor mentioned in Rank Math's advisory. The PHP script also includes the ability to execute commands, modify WordPress databases, and steal AWS, Cloudflare, Google Cloud, Azure credentials, SSH keys, and other sensitive information. While these IoCs indicate it is connected to the same threat actor as the Rank Math attack, BleepingComputer could not confirm whether it was distributed through the compromised plugin. Cleanup recommendations Website administrators who suspect a compromise should restore website files and the database from a clean backup, run security scans, and rotate all passwords, keys, and salts. For websites without a safe backup to restore from, Rank Math recommends manual cleanup, noting that deactivating or updating the plugin after a compromise will not remove the threat. Cleanup requires deleting the entire plugin folder and malicious database entries before investigating additional backdoors, unauthorized administrator accounts, altered files, scheduled tasks, and possible changes outside WordPress. It is also recommended to block all outbound connections to the attacker's rank1cdn[.]com domain. Users who installed but never activated the plugin should now delete it, download the clean 3.0.124 version, and then scan their sites. BleepingComputer contacted Rank Math for details on the number of potentially affected sites and the initial attack vector but had received no response by the time of publication. 1l6u5zh.text: A Northern California federal judge ruled that WhatsApp failed to prove a prominent spyware company violated a court injunction requiring it to stop using the messaging app’s infrastructure to mount snooping attacks on customers. The ruling Friday by Judge Phyllis Hamilton was in response to an appeal WhatsApp filed in June. The Meta-owned messaging service wanted the judge to hold the NSO Group — maker of the powerful zero-click Pegasus spyware deployed against 1,400 app users in 2019 — in contempt for what WhatsApp called spearphishing attacks against individuals. Hamilton issued the injunction against NSO in 2025 and fined it $4.4 million, agreeing with WhatsApp that the spyware maker had improperly abused its infrastructure to target and, in some cases, infect users’ devices with spyware. Despite winning the overall case, however, WhatsApp failed to convince Hamilton that NSO had violated the injunction because it did not provide enough “clear and convincing evidence” of the alleged misbehavior, the judge said. “In the court’s view, plaintiffs took a calculated risk in choosing to limit the level of detail in their supporting evidence,” Hamilton’s opinion said. WhatsApp put forward evidence that solely relied on the testimony of Andrew Blaich, a security engineer investigator on Meta’s threat intelligence team. Blaich submitted a declaration that alleged he found 23 new Whatsapp accounts carrying “technical and behavioral signatures that Meta has previously associated with NSO testing, including account registration patterns, device and other related information, and connections to known NSO-controlled infrastructure,” according to the opinion, quoting from Blaich’s declaration. WhatsApp told Hamilton it was concerned about providing specifics about how Blaich found the activity because divulging methods could make it much harder for the tech giant to fight spyware companies in the future. In September 2024, Apple dropped a suit against NSO because it said continuing the case risked exposing “vital security information.” Digital freedoms advocates condemned the decision Hamilton issued Friday, saying it would be self-sabotage for WhatsApp to unveil its tracking protocols publicly. “Judges working on spyware cases should consider in making these decisions that WhatsApp exposing its own research and detection methods could provide enormous benefits to NSO, as well as foreign intelligence services, exploit developers and criminals that can learn how sophisticated spyware is detected and how platforms operate,” Natalia Krapiva, senior tech-counsel at Access Now told Recorded Future News via text message. Krapiva said that requiring such disclosures in order to hold NSO accountable would “lead to complete impunity for the spyware industry.” WhatsApp and NSO Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment. No previous articleNo new articlesSuzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

1uixozp.text: IT management software company ConnectWise shut down several of its services this weekend after Microsoft and other cybersecurity companies warned of a supply chain attack impacting its cloud backup system. ConnectWise initially said on Friday that it was investigating “attempts of unauthorized access associated with the ConnectWise Cloud Backup environment,” and confirmed such access on Saturday. Incident responders at cybersecurity firm Huntress said a credential belonging to ConnectWise Cloud Backup was compromised and used to gain access to the customers’ Microsoft 365 environment. Microsoft confirmed in its own statement that threat actors “likely abused permissions previously granted by customers to the application, including highly elevated permissions like Directory.ReadWrite.All.” ConnectWise Cloud Backup is a cloud-based backup and recovery service designed to help protect data in Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace. The tool needs broad access to mailboxes, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams and other data, according to Huntress. An attacker using stolen ConnectWise Cloud Backup credentials will inherently have wide access to any systems where the app is installed, including places where no trail of evidence will be left. ConnectWise did not respond to requests for comment about the attackers or about how many customers were impacted. A spokesperson told Recorded Future News that there is “no indication" that backup data was compromised. The current service interruptions apply to the cloud backup system as well as the SaaS Security and Cloud Management platforms. “We have remediated identified compromised credentials and identities, and we continue authentication monitoring, permission review, and forensic analysis,” the spokesperson said. In multiple updates throughout Saturday and Sunday, ConnectWise said it revoked certificates used for affected application connections across all users. This removed ConnectWise’s access through those connections and all shared credentials previously used for Cloud Backup are no longer valid and cannot be used. The company said they do not have visibility into partner and customer environments, so they cannot determine whether a particular customer’s Microsoft 365 environment was breached. ConnectWise said since taking a range of actions, it has seen no successful threat activity. There is no timeline for a restoration of services, the spokesperson said. Waves of attacks Huntress incident responders said they initially saw password spray attacks against four law firms on October 13 and 14. By October 15, about 50 systems monitored by Huntress saw attackers use ConnectWise's Cloud Management apps to assign themselves directory or administrative roles. In total, Huntress saw unauthorized sign-ins in 162 tenants. Huntress also saw a second targeted wave of largely unsuccessful attacks targeting systems “in the policy, national security, trade, and critical mineral sectors.” “Unlike the first wave of activity outlined in our initial blog below, most of these tenants do not rely on any ConnectWise products. In tenants without the relevant ConnectWise service principal, the attempts failed because the application was not present,” Huntress explained. Like Huntress, Microsoft and other cybersecurity firms said they observed “broad” attacks starting on October 15. Huntress warned that backup services like ConnectWise Cloud Backup normally hold read access to mail, files, Teams, and directory data so it can copy them and restore them. “The larger risk is what happens when that access is used to gain more. If an application can assign directory roles, as we saw in one tenant, it can make itself a Global Administrator, and an administrator can add credentials to other applications, create new applications and grant them permissions, reset passwords and authentication methods for users, and change Conditional Access policies,” Huntress added. “Each of those steps gives the attacker another way back in that does not depend on the original vendor credential, which is why rotating the vendor credential is necessary, but not enough.” They noted that in managed service providers the effect can be even worse — with attackers using their foothold in one customer to gain access to all other customers. ConnectWise has dealt with multiple security incidents in the past, including one last year involving a nation-state attack on its remote management and monitoring software that impacted some of its customers. Cybercriminals previously exploited multiple vulnerabilities in the company’s products that led to ransomware attacks. No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

1dr4wxj.text: Hackers reportedly compromised AOMEI's servers to distribute malware through a built-in promotional feature in its backup software, briefly tampering with configuration files before restoring them to their original state to hide the attacks. The supply chain attacks took place between April and July 2026 and targeted the update and notification systems used by AOMEI Backupper, a Windows application for backing up data, cloning disks, and restoring systems. Researchers at ManageEngine's Threat Analysis Lab (METAL), working with Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, uncovered the campaign and investigated the attacks. In reports published by Google and ManageEngine, the activity is attributed to a threat actor tracked as UNC7017, who used the compromised infrastructure to distribute a previously unknown malware downloader called CROSSROAD and a backdoor named SHINYROAD. The researchers identified affected organizations in multiple countries, including the United States, Australia, India, Singapore, Spain, and Switzerland, across sectors such as IT services, telecommunications, and higher education. However, Google warned that the attacks were opportunistic and could have affected additional organizations that checked for software updates during the brief periods when malicious files were being distributed. Software The attacks were first detected on May 28, when ManageEngine said its endpoint security software spotted AOMEI Backupper suddenly installing the legitimate remote administration tool Radmin on computers at two unrelated companies in different countries. The Radmin installation was suspicious because AOMEI's built-in promotion processes launched it, which normally handle downloading and displaying promotional content and notifications. However, when researchers attempted to reproduce the behavior on their own test systems, they found nothing malicious. Instead, the software contacted AOMEI's servers and downloaded the legitimate configuration file. Further testing showed that instead of permanently replacing files on AOMEI's servers, the attackers briefly modified two configuration files used by the promotion and notification systems: https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/down_html.ini https://account.aomeitech.com/Notifycfg.ini The first file, down_html.ini, tells AOMEI Backupper where to download update packages. The second, Notifycfg.ini, controls notifications and can trigger content to run on the computer. By modifying these files, the attackers redirected the software to download a malicious ZIP archive and then used the notification mechanism to execute the malware without requiring user interaction. Researchers at Google later confirmed this execution flow in their own tests. AOMEI supply chain attack execution flowSource: Google After failing to reproduce the original attack, ManageEngine began continuously monitoring AOMEI's servers. On July 16, that monitoring finally captured the malicious modifications as they happened, confirming that AOMEI's systems were serving the malicious content. The researchers also found that the attackers had modified the expected checksum in the update configuration, allowing the malicious archive to pass the software's file verification checks. Google and ManageEngine say they identified three windows where the malicious configuration file was being sent by Aomei's servers: May 28: 10-minute exposure window (05:40 – 05:50 UTC) July 16: 6-minute exposure window (08:33 – 08:39 UTC) July 20: 5-minute exposure window (10:35 – 10:40 UTC) The attackers restored the configuration files back to its original form within minutes, making the compromise difficult to detect. During these windows, the malicious configuration file was used to install the CROSSROAD and SHINYROAD malware. When launched, the CROSSROAD downloader checked the performed reconnasaince on the infected computer, downloaded additional components, and established persistence through a scheduled task. SHINYROAD is a backdoor that used legitimate Radmin components to load malicious code and establish an outbound connection to an attacker-controlled command-and-control server. This allowed the attackers to potentially execute additional commands and payloads on compromised computers. During the July 20 attack, Google also observed a second technique that attempted to steal Windows authentication hashes by forcing the software's notification system to access an attacker-controlled WebDAV resource through an invisible popup. This technique could expose NTLM hashes that can be collected by the attacker-controlled server and later cracked using various tools. The researchers also identified several IP addresses and hostnames used during the attacks, including 8.210.84[.]56, serv.oss-cn-hongkong[.]aliyuncs.com, hostnames under storage-data[.]com, and storage.googleapis.com, a legitimate Google Cloud Storage endpoint. AOMEI says CTO is investigating ManageEngine told BleepingComputer that it first notified AOMEI about the suspicious activity on June 7, more than a month before researchers directly captured the malicious configuration files being served from its servers. At the time, AOMEI initially suggested that the content may have been intercepted and modified while in transit, an explanation the researchers disagreed with. "The evidence did not support AOMEI’s explanation of interception in transit," reads ManageEngine's report. "Both endpoints had retrieved the content over HTTPS from AOMEI-owned hostnames, across different countries and unrelated network paths, and the executable had arrived through the application’s own extraction sequence rather than being written directly to disk by an external process. The content had been altered before it reached either endpoint, within the vendor-hosted delivery path." When ManageEngine captured another attack on July 16, it immediately provided AOMEI with the original and modified file hashes, file differences, and altered files. "AOMEI engaged, conducted its own review, and told us its initial examination had not found evidence of a breach," ManageEngine told BleepingComputer. The researchers said AOMEI indicated that it planned to move the affected configuration files to new infrastructure with more detailed logging. ManageEngine told BleepingComputer it advised AOMEI to preserve existing evidence before making those changes and to bring in incident-response specialists, connecting the company with Mandiant to assist with the investigation. AOMEI later informed the researchers that its technical team had upgraded its servers, patched potential vulnerabilities, and verified that the files hosted on its infrastructure were correct. Google also confirmed in its report that Mandiant notified AOMEI about the configuration file tampering on July 17 and that the company responded on July 29th, stating it took corrective action. When contacted by BleepingComputer about the findings, AOMEI said it was treating the matter as a high priority and that its chief technology officer was leading an internal investigation. "We have also internally detected this report and have classified it as a high-priority matter. Our CTO is currently leading a dedicated investigation to ensure accurate issue identification," AOMEI told BleepingComputer. The company said its CTO would provide a more detailed response about the incident and the investigation's progress, and BleepingComputer will update this article if we receive new information. AOMEI did not immediately confirm how attackers gained access to its update infrastructure or whether the reported compromise had been fully resolved. While AOMEI says it has secured its servers, ManageEngine warns that these changes would not remove malware previously installed on customers' computers. "A server-side fix stops new infections; it does not remove the backdoor from machines that received it during an earlier window," ManageEngine told BleepingComputer. Organizations using AOMEI Backupper are advised to review the indicators of compromise published by Google and ManageEngine, including suspicious scheduled tasks, unexpected executable files in AOMEI installation directories, and connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure. 1tocq79.text: Staffing software company Bullhorn has disabled access to its platform to contain a cyberattack that caused a system-wide outage. The company says it has isolated the issue and eradicated the immediate threat. Currently, its team is working to restore services following thorough security reviews conducted with help from CrowdStrike specialists. Bullhorn is an American software company specializing in cloud-based staffing and recruitment solutions. Its platform helps staffing firms manage the recruitment lifecycle, including candidate tracking, onboarding, and payroll. The company says it serves more than 10,000 customers worldwide. According to a status page on the incident, customers started to experience issues with job posting in the Bullhorn application on Friday. The next day, the company said it was "experiencing a system-wide outage affecting the Bullhorn platform," and later confirmed that the issues were caused by a cyberattack. "We have detected a cyber incident on the Bullhorn Platform. We have temporarily disabled access to our systems in order to contain the activity while we investigate further," the company said in an update. In a FAQ page, Bullhorn says that a forensic investigation has been started and "not yet determined whether customer data was exfiltrated." Bullhorn promised to notify affected individuals directly if a data breach is confirmed. According to the firm’s status page, most of the services are under maintainance or have degraded performance, except for Adapt, eEmpACT, and StaffSuite, which remain operational. Major outages affect ATS/CRM, Automation, Back Office, Talent Platform, and sandbox environments. At the time of writing, degraded performance was reported for Bullhorn for Salesforce and associated products, Onboarding365, and additional solutions including Amplify, Analytics, Messaging, SourceBreaker, VMS Sync, Data Hub, Erecruit, SalesDuel, and VMS Access. Bullhorn has not provided any timelines for when those services will be restored. Customers should check the company’s service status page for the latest updates. Also, the latest update mentions that all non-SSO users will be required to reset their passwords on their next login. Also, as per the FAQ page, API passwords require rotation to protect integrations, while client-secret changes will follow later. For Bullhorn-hosted instances, this will take place automatically. Customers can request data exports through the firm’s support to minimize business disruption. Unposted time records will be reprocessed after restoration, and service credits will be reviewed against applicable SLAs once the incident is resolved. BleepingComputer has contacted Bullhorn to request more information about the attack, and we will update this post with their response when received. 172rwqb.text: Another Serbian opposition leader’s phone was discovered to have been infected with powerful spyware, the latest in a series of such discoveries in the lead-up to national elections next week. The digital forensics research institute the Citizen Lab confirmed on Monday that University of Belgrade Rector Vladan Đokić’s phone was infected with Pegasus spyware sometime this year. Đokić has been a vocal supporter of a student protest movement calling for the permanent removal from government of Serbia’s former president, Aleksandar Vučić. Vučić, who left the presidency just weeks ago due to term limits, is running for prime minister in elections to be held on October 25 and is widely expected to wrest back control of the country if reelected to a role he previously held from 2014-2017. A second suspected victim’s device is still being analyzed by the Citizen Lab. Rade Bajić, a prosecutor who investigated alleged corruption involving a Vučić effort to sell a protected historic building to U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, received an Apple threat notification in August, according to a press release from Serbia’s SHARE Foundation. Apple notifications are widely considered high-confidence indicators of commercial spyware targeting. The Serbian authorities have been using NSO Group’s Pegasus against regime opponents for some time. In 2026, the SHARE Foundation, along with the Citizen Lab and Amnesty International, have so far found that at least 15 people have been targeted with advanced spyware, according to the press release. The continued use of Pegasus to target members of Serbian civil society battling an authoritarian regime raises significant questions about NSO Group’s repeated assurances that it does not do business with repressive governments that abuse its technology. A spokesperson for the company did not respond to comment nor did a spokesperson for the Serbian embassy in Washington. Serbian student protests have rocked Belgrade since November 2024 when anti-corruption demonstrations began. In recent months, several other students and journalists have been found to have been targeted with spyware. “There’s been increasing physical and digital repression,” said Adrijana Ristić, a researcher at the SHARE Foundation. “The targeting has been very broad, not just in the sense of spyware — there's confidential communications leaking… and attacks on journalists as well.” “The tensions are very high at this moment.” Đokić is well-known for “refusing to facilitate a government-led crackdown on student protesters, which led to intense pressure from the Serbian authorities,” according to the Citizen Lab, which said Serbian authorities raided his offices, seizing computers and servers, in late March. Bajić, the prosecutor who received an Apple notification for spyware, helped kill a deal between Vučić and Kushner for a Belgrade Trump Tower and charged government officials after finding forged documents underpinning the negotiations, Ristić said. The Trump Tower project was planned to be built on the ruins of a protected cultural heritage site in the capital, the Citizen Lab said. Bajić was transferred off the case in November 2025 with no explanation. In February, he spoke out against political repression at a demonstration. A month later other prosecutors filed an indictment against the country’s current Minister of Culture and three other senior government officials on charges relating to the failed Trump Tower deal. The regime has been going after him for at least a year, he said. In November 2025, Vučić personally referred to him on state-run television as a “criminal from the Prosecutor’s Office for Organized Crime,” Bajić said. ‘It is evident that all of this is being done because our Prosecutor’s Office is conducting criminal proceedings against representatives of the executive branch of government,” he said. “My involvement in this case was the sole reason for this unlawful spyware attack.” No previous articleNo new articlesSuzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

14m48xt.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 19, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security Threat actors have begun to exploit a chain of vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server to deploy cryptocurrency miners and reverse proxy software, a day after a proof-of-concept (PoC) went public. According to a researcher who goes by the online alias boredhackerblog, the exploitation activity involves chaining four different vulnerabilities, collectively called Plex2Shell. The vulnerabilities are below - CVE-2026-96652 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An unauthenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) stemming via the "/player/timeline" endpoint by taking advantage of the fact that the "protocol" parameter is inserted into a programmatically-constructed player URL with no validation, allowing an attacker to force the Plex server to POST to a destination of their choice. CVE-2026-96654 (CVSS score: 6.9) - An improper neutralization of URL values included in the "searchOne" endpoint that could allow an attacker to call other plugins' functions and supply their own parameters to obtain the owner's admin token. CVE-2026-96655 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An SSRF vulnerability that allows an authenticated user (i.e., the owner token) to request arbitrary internal or external addresses (e.g., an attacker-hosted carrier video carrying the malicious ELF payload) via the '/video/:/transcode/universal' path parameter. CVE-2026-96656 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An external control of file name or path vulnerability that allows the ELF shared object to an attacker-chosen path in the Codecs directory and execute it. Put differently, the vulnerabilities can be combined together in this order to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on susceptible Plex Media Server instances. The vulnerabilities, along with CVE-2026-96651 (CVSS score: 7.1), were disclosed to Plex on July 27, 2026, by security researcher Zach Main, and were patched in Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 released on August 3, 2026. In-the-wild exploitation attempts targeting the flaws have since been recorded a day after technical details of the Plex2Shell chain went public on October 16, 2026. The attacks led to the deployment of a miner payload from a remote server ("217.60.194[.]116"). The attack efforts have been observed from the following IP addresses - 91.92.40[.]202 176.65.139[.]228 45.194.92[.]222 176.65.139[.]228 Furthermore, the vulnerabilities have been exploited to deliver an artifact named "myawesomeproxy," which, according to VirusTotal, is a stealthy Linux backdoor and reverse proxy. Running the program displays the below message, per boredhackerblog - Running this software on any of your devices makes you agree to the potential external use of your internet traffic. Also deployed concurrently is an XMRig miner process identified as "mylovelyminer" with its mining server pointing to "ota.proxystream[.]st." Notably, another subdomain associated with the same domain, "global.relay.proxystream[.]st," was flagged by Bitsight in August 2026 in connection with the AISURU DDoS and proxyware botnet. Posts on Reddit indicate that multiple Plex users have had their instances compromised with the same "mylovelyminer" payload. That said, it's not known at this stage if it stems from the exploitation of Plex2Shell flaws. The development comes more than a month after Plex urged users to update their instances to the latest version following the release of an update that addressed multiple unspecified security flaws. It's unclear if the aforementioned vulnerabilities were part of this alert. The Hacker News has contacted Plex for comment and we will update the story if we hear back. In light of active exploitation, users are advised to keep their Plex installations up-to-date for optimal protection.

ngye1r.text: The open-source AI coding project OpenCode has notified some users that stored API keys they used with external providers were exposed in a security breach. Multiple users reported that the incident led to unauthorized API charges and suspended projects in Google Cloud. According to the project maintainer, the breach affected 1.4% of OpenCode Console users, with some reporting more than $1,700 in unauthorized charges overnight. OpenCode is a model-agnostic AI coding agent that helps users understand code, write features, and fix bugs using natural-language instructions, through a terminal, desktop app, or code editor. Users can connect AI models from multiple AI providers to the OpenCode console to streamline and automate the development process. Distillation attack On Saturday, OpenCode announced that it suffered a large distillation attack that impacted only developers who linked external providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. “We had a security breach last night related to a large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users,” the project maintainer said. “We have notified them all this morning via email. If you did not get an email, you were not impacted, it was a subset of users who had external providers linked.” Distillation is a legitimate machine-learning technique that trains smaller AI models using responses generated by more powerful models. The goal is to create cheaper, faster models that retain many of the capabilities of their larger counterparts. However, the technique becomes an attack when it involves large-scale training through unauthorized queries. OpenCode co-founder Dax Raad said attackers had been targeting the company's systems for at least 48 hours using AI agents. He also said OpenCode's investigation of the attackers were blocked when the AI models it was using began refusing requests due to built-in security safeguards. Distillation attack on OpenCode ran for 48 hourssource: Dax Raad Raad said the situation stabilized after OpenCode began using OpenAI’s Daybreak AI cybersecurity model for defensive work, which it was approved to use on Saturday. The email sent to impacted users notes that the earliest possible exposure of the users’ keys was on October 17, 2026, 00:30 UTC, and that no data appears to have been exposed. OpenCode also said it was working with Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic to address the incident but could not share further details at this time. User reports claim rogue charges following the private key leaks, ranging from several hundred USD to up to $1,700. OpenCode’s message to impacted users mentions the possibility of reimbursement for those impacted. Some users reported that Google suspended their projects after detecting "abusive activity consistent with hijacked resources.” BleepingComputer contacted OpenCode for more details, but we have not heard back as of publication. kvw5m2.text: Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch multinational grocery chain, said Monday that a cyberattack forced it to take systems offline across most of its U.S. and European brands, impacting shoppers on both sides of the Atlantic. The company confirmed that the suspicious activity it announced detecting in its IT systems last week was caused by malicious actors, adding that it filed a police report in the Netherlands on Monday. The incident disrupted online services in the U.S., Netherlands and Belgium, although stores remained open. Although the company said it had no evidence that sensitive customer, employee or partner data was stolen, it cautioned that the investigation into the hack remains ongoing. It did not describe the nature of the attack, nor whether a ransom was involved, stating: “We are not sharing further details that could compromise security measures or interfere with our response efforts.” The retailer said it was restoring services in phases, and that online shopping services at U.S. brands — including Food Lion and Stop & Shop — are not yet functional, although they are expected to resume in the coming days. The websites and apps for Dutch brands Albert Heijn, Etos and Gall & Gall are back online, though Albert Heijn home deliveries are not expected to resume until Friday. It said e-commerce services have been restored in Belgium and Central and Southeastern Europe. Chief Executive Officer Frans Muller apologized for the disruption, saying taking systems offline was a necessary precaution. “Although this incident was caused by the malicious actions of others, we apologize for the inconvenience this has caused — especially to our customers,” Muller said. The company said it notified Dutch cybersecurity authorities within 24 hours of detecting the incident. Ahold Delhaize previously suffered a cyberattack in 2024, causing issues at prominent supermarkets across the U.S. More than 2.2 million people had information stolen from the company’s systems during that incident. 1v2pf25.text: Copies of Rank Math PRO, the paid version of the Rank Math SEO plugin for WordPress, that were downloaded from rankmath.com or delivered as updates between 20:02 UTC on October 15 and 07:12 UTC on October 16 contained malware, Rank Math said in a security notice published on October 16. Any site that installed and activated one of those copies should be treated as compromised, and the malware can recreate its hidden backdoor whenever someone visits the site. Rank Math has removed the affected files and released a clean version, 3.0.124. Installing it replaces the plugin but does not remove files, administrator accounts, or scheduled tasks the malware may already have placed elsewhere on the server, Wordfence said in an advisory on October 17. Who Is Affected The version number does not show whether a copy is affected. Rank Math's changelog dates 3.0.123 to October 7, more than a week before the window opened, and the notice limits the incident to copies downloaded or installed through an update during the window. A copy of 3.0.123 obtained before 20:02 UTC on October 15 is outside it. The notice sorts sites into three cases: You installed and activated 3.0.123 during the window: treat the site as compromised, even if it has since been updated to 3.0.124, and follow the recovery steps below. You installed it but never activated it: delete the plugin files, install 3.0.124 from your Rank Math account, and run a security scan. You downloaded it but never installed or activated it: nothing in this incident alone indicates the site was compromised. Rank Math has emailed some users about the incident and told anyone unsure whether the files were installed or activated to contact its support team. The notice applies only to the PRO plugin, which customers download and update from rankmath.com rather than WordPress.org. The free Rank Math SEO plugin on WordPress.org, which lists more than 4 million active installations and was last updated on October 6, is not named in it. What the Malware Does What is known about the malware comes from Rank Math's notice. Neither it nor Wordfence's advisory includes an analysis of the code, and neither names who is behind it. Deleting suspicious files before stopping what recreates the backdoor may not resolve the problem, which is why the cleanup order below matters. The attacker may also have left PHP backdoor files in other plugins' folders, in theme folders, and in the must-use plugins directory, created administrator accounts, added a fake WordPress core file, changed .htaccess so that .cache files run as PHP, and added scheduled tasks and SSH keys. Any password, database credential, API key, or other secret the site could reach may have been exposed, and owners should assume it was. Wordfence assigned the incident CVE-2026-111862 and rates it 9.8 out of 10, with the researcher listed as unknown. Patchstack classifies it as a backdoor and says that, because the attack was on Rank Math's own systems, "a rule is not possible for mitigation." How to Recover Rank Math's preferred recovery is a restore. Where a backup of the site and its database from before 20:02 UTC on October 15 exists, restore it, run a security scan, change every password and credential, and only then install 3.0.124 from your Rank Math account. Where no clean backup exists, the manual cleanup runs in a fixed order, and three actions come before anything else is touched: Delete the entire rank-math-pro plugin folder using the hosting file manager or FTP. "Deactivating the plugin alone is not sufficient," the notice says. In the wp_options table, delete any entry whose option_name is _uf6qdn2hmm, t8krdk990phb or _np5pvf754c. Block outgoing connections to rank1cdn[.]com if the hosting provider or firewall allows it. Only then does the search for other changes begin, in these places: Files: PHP files in wp-content/mu-plugins/, in other plugins' folders, in the inc/, includes/ and lib/ folders of non-default themes, in Rank Math's own includes/ folder, and in uploads/. Code: PHP that uses base64_decode with XOR loops, the key xmmqhn, proc_open, or PHP-FPM socket code. File: wp-includes/class-wp-cache-util.php, which is not a WordPress core file. Accounts: administrator usernames beginning wpsupport_, or accounts with email addresses ending @wp-mail[.]net. Server: .htaccess rules that let .cache files run as PHP, .cache files containing PHP code, entries tagged #ms6v46 in the web server user's crontab, WordPress scheduled events, SSH authorized_keys files, other users' crontabs, running processes, and any location outside the site where the web server can write. Wordfence adds a caution: "Their absence does not, by itself, prove that a website is clean." Credentials are changed in every case, even after a restore from backup. The list covers WordPress passwords, the database username and password in wp-config.php, the security keys and salts in the same file, payment gateway, SMTP and other API keys, hosting control panel, FTP, SFTP and SSH access, secrets held in environment variables, and two-factor authentication for administrators. The cleanup ends with a security scan, wp core verify-checksums for WordPress core, and wp plugin verify-checksums --all, with the caution that checksums may not exist for premium plugins. WordPress.org publishes none for this one. The Hacker News checked its plugin-checksums service on October 19 and found no file for the PRO plugin under either of its names, while the service does publish one for the free plugin. The fallback notice provides a clean copy from the official source. The clean 3.0.124 goes on last, downloaded by logging in at rankmath.com directly. Some customers may be unable to log in and may need to reset their account password, the notice says, without saying why, and Rank Math will never send login or download links by email. What Rank Math Has Not Said Rank Math, part of the Swedish hosting group group.one, has not said how the malicious files entered its download and update system, how many customers received one, whether automatic updates delivered them, or what the clean and tainted packages' hashes are. Its only statement about the future is that the team is taking steps to reduce the risk of similar incidents. Registry records show the domain Rank Math tells owners to block, rank1cdn[.]com, was registered at 19:31 UTC on October 14, about a day before the window opened. A Pattern This Year This is at least the third time this year that a premium WordPress plugin's vendor-run update channel has delivered backdoored builds. In April, Nextend's update system served a backdoored Smart Slider 3 Pro for about six hours. In June, ShapedPlugin's Pro plugins were found to have been backdoored in its update channel, and one package that had shipped clean was later "tampered with under the same version number," the trap Rank Math's customers now face. Attackers also altered scripts served from Awesome Motive's CDN in June and poisoned BdThemes' API feed in August. Nothing published links the attackers behind any of those incidents to this one.

6ruo6m.text: Thousands of Russian users reported problems accessing the country's largest social network, VKontakte, and its music streaming service over the weekend following a Ukrainian drone strike on a data center near St. Petersburg. The disruptions began Sunday, when users complained of difficulties loading news feeds, playing music and accessing other features of VK's platforms. VK confirmed that its facility in the Leningrad region was targeted in the overnight attack on October 18 but denied that the incident had affected its services, saying they remained available as usual. The company did not disclose the extent of the damage or how many servers were affected. Independent monitoring services, however, recorded a surge in user complaints and a decline in VK's network connectivity. It was not immediately clear whether the disruptions were caused by the strike. Outage-tracking website Downdetector received approximately 6,600 reports of problems with VK's services on Sunday, including about 600 within a single hour. Another Russian monitoring service, Sboy, registered roughly 2,100 complaints. Internet monitoring organization NetBlocks reported that connectivity associated with VK had fallen to 56% of normal levels during the incident. By Monday, the number of complaints had declined, according to Russian monitoring service Detector404, although users continued to report problems uploading photos and videos, streaming music, logging into their accounts and sending messages. Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point said Ukrainian forces used its FP-1 drones to strike several targets in the region, including VK's data center. The company claimed the facility had sustained significant damage, although VK has not confirmed the extent of the destruction. According to Fire Point, the facility is one of VKontakte's key data centers, responsible for storing and processing user data, including photos, videos and other content. The company cited previously published figures indicating that the site housed more than 20,000 servers in 640 racks. Ukrainian media outlets and open-source intelligence analysts reported that the strike caused extensive damage to the building, including the partial collapse of its roof. Those reports could not be independently verified. Pavel Durov, who co-founded VKontakte before leaving Russia and launching Telegram, said Sunday that he had built the data center about 15 years ago, and it was sold to VK a few years later. "They failed to protect it," he wrote. VK is one of Russia's largest technology companies, operating the social networks VKontakte and Odnoklassniki, Mail.ru email services and the government-backed Max messaging app, among other products. The reported outages come amid repeated attacks on data centers in Russia and Ukraine. Earlier in October, Ukrainian forces struck data centers belonging to Russian technology giant Yandex three times. Following the third reported attack, users across Russia experienced problems accessing Yandex services and numerous other websites. A data center belonging to Sberbank, Russia's majority state-owned banking giant, was also reportedly targeted in a separate attack. Russia has also repeatedly struck Ukrainian data centers in recent weeks, damaging infrastructure used by businesses and telecommunications providers. On Monday, Ukrainian telecommunications operator Datagroup said a Russian ballistic missile strike had destroyed equipment and infrastructure at one of its Kyiv data centers, leaving the facility beyond repair. Russian attacks in September damaged at least six Ukrainian data centers, including facilities operated by MiroHost, Parkovyi, UTELS and Pavutyna. Moscow has claimed that Ukrainian data centers were being used to support the country's armed forces. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

1vngtuh.text: Microsoft has fixed a known issue that caused games and Windows 11 apps using AC-3 (Dolby Digital) audio decoding to crash after installing the September 2026 preview update (KB5124010). While KB5124010 is an optional update that requires clicking a "Download and install" link (reducing the number of potentially affected Windows users), it installs automatically on devices where the "Get the latest updates as soon as they're available" option is toggled on. "In some cases the application can fail to launch, or close without warning. In other cases the application will work normally until certain features are used, such as playing music," Microsoft said when it acknowledged this issue two weeks ago. "Affected applications may vary and can include games, media players, and certain productivity applications." However, it added that many modern apps that don't use Windows' built-in audio decoding for this type of encoding aren't affected, and that modern apps that use the legacy AC-3 codec often include their own audio decoding components. In a new update to the Windows release health dashboard, Microsoft said the KB5127648 October 2026 Patch Tuesday update addresses this known issue and advised affected users to install it on affected systems running Windows 11 24H2 and later. "We recommend you install the latest security update for your device as it contains important improvements and issue resolutions, including this one," it said. Over the last several years, Microsoft has resolved multiple other audio issues impacting various software and Windows components. For instance, two years ago it confirmed a bug that caused game audio to unexpectedly jump to full volume when using USB DAC sound systems and blocked Windows 24H2 upgrades on devices with incompatible Intel Smart Sound Technology (SST) audio drivers because of blue screen of death (BSOD) issues. Last year, in January 2025, Microsoft addressed a similar issue that triggered audio playback problems on Windows 11 24H2 systems with USB audio device drivers and lifted a safeguard hold preventing upgrades because an incompatibility issue caused Bluetooth headsets and speakers to malfunction on systems with Dirac audio improvement software. More recently, in September, Microsoft released emergency updates to fix another bug that triggered USB audio issues after installing the September 2026 KB5124008 and KB5124012 security updates. istocc.text: The worst problems don't always come with a warning. Sometimes they arrive through a service everyone trusts, a device someone bought, or a system nobody thought to check. By the time something looks wrong, the damage may already be done. This week had plenty of that. Trusted connections became a problem. Hardware wasn't as safe as it looked. Old bugs found new victims, and some systems were left so exposed that breaking in barely required any effort. Even AI agents crossed lines they weren't supposed to. Some attacks were clever. Others were painfully simple. The full recap shows just how much can go wrong, and how little it sometimes takes. ⚡ Threat of the Week ConnectWise Suspends Cloud Backup Following Unauthorized Access — ConnectWise disabled seven ConnectWise application identities as it continues its investigation into an incident in which unknown threat actors obtained unauthorized access to the application identities and compromised Microsoft 365 tenants. The IT management software provider said it took the action on October 17, 2026, at 07:00 UTC, adding it has also suspended Cloud Backup service by revoking certificates used for affected application connections across all users. 🔔 Top News BeyondTrust Remote Support Flaw Exploited as 0-Day — The China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (previously UNC5221 or Warp Panda) exploited a newly disclosed security flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) as a zero-day in late August 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS score: 9.3), is a case of improper origin validation in an internal messaging component that could be exploited by a remote attacker to perform file operations on an affected appliance. According to Google-owned Mandiant, the attack involved the deployment of a lightweight PHP web shell codenamed SAWFLY for interactive remote access and a tunneling program called BARECLAW to route traffic through the device. Only a small number of organizations are assessed to be impacted. Microsoft Disrupts 3 Phishing Kits Linked to Over 1 Billion Scam Messages — Microsoft says it has dismantled a criminal marketplace that sold three phishing kits, namely CoGUI (aka NX or FA), Haozi (aka Phoenix), and Iron Man System, that were responsible for sending over 1 billion malicious messages to more than 75,000 organizations worldwide. Redmond said it took down Yam Store (aka Storm-3119), a coordinated underground network that offered commercial phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) toolkits that allowed other threat actors to readily purchase and deploy phishing pages and steal data and credentials. The kits were also capable of advanced evasion, such as geofencing, fake CAPTCHA gates, IP address blocklists and allowlists, and anti-detection configurations. Yam Store functioned as an initial access broker, peddling not just phishing kits but also infrastructure built on compromised or fraudulently obtained Microsoft and Google cloud environments. Ledger Finds Unauthorized Hardware Implants — Cryptocurrency hardware maker Ledger temporarily paused sales of its products via CryptoBilis and other third-party resellers in Southeast Asia and Germany after a backdoor embedded into a handful of wallets led to the theft of an estimated $100 million in cryptocurrency. The implants are said to be an advanced version of a backdoor that hardware hacker Joe Grand found earlier this year and notified Ledger in March 2026. It's not clear how this occurred, but signs point to a compromise of Ledger's supply chain. One of the victims of the incident is a fraudster who engaged in a task scam and lost more than $4.8 million. "In this task scam, people were paid to fake sales and reviews of real items," Chainalysis said. "Then a 'negative balance' appeared, and they were told to add their own money in order to get paid. On Sep 22, the person behind the scam moved the proceeds into three separate Ledger addresses. On Oct 9, thieves emptied all three. One transfer each, into the same wallet." According to cybersecurity journalist Kim Zetter, Trezor wallet devices sold by third-party non-authorized sellers have also been found to contain implants that generated pre-determined seed phrases so as to allow the attackers to guess them easily and gain access to the accounts. Pwn2Own Ireland Demos 98 0-Days — The Pwn2Own Ireland 2026 hacking contest saw white-hat hackers exploiting 98 zero-day flaws, earning them a collective $1,262,000 in rewards. Ikotas Labs came first with 42.5 Master of Pwn points and $361,000 in cash after discovering 12 unique bugs. Xint and Team ZyGoat secured second and third spots. Ikotas Labs, Xint, and Mobile Hacking Lab broke into Google's Pixel 10, earning them $150,000, $300,000, and $112,500, respectively. Vendors are expected to patch the zero-days disclosed during the competition within 90 days before the details are publicly disclosed. OpenAI Disclosed New Misalignment Cases — OpenAI said internal models hacked more websites, bypassed browsing restrictions, and used cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn't otherwise access, in the latest set of disclosures where its agents carried out unethical and likely illegal acts. In all, the company reported seven new incidents. The development came as the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it received "multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers" whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, accessed personal data from Indian organizations. The agents found their way in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations. OpenAI Engineer Charged — The U.S. Department of Justice charged an OpenAI engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, with attempting to intercept oral communications after allegedly planting a recording device in an executive conference room. Prosecutors claimed company security staff found a second device in his bag. CCTV footage placed the defendant near the conference room on several dates. Alfozan allegedly had no authority to access or participate in meetings held in the room, which is often reserved for the highest-level discussions. In a subsequent filing, federal prosecutors revealed that Alfozan had booked a one-way ticket from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia with his wife and a third family member before his arrest on October 9, 2026. Attacks on French Refrigeration Systems — Cyber attacks on Danfoss- and Copeland-managed refrigeration systems pushed temperatures as high as 50°C (122°F) for roughly six hours, impacting over 700 French supermarkets and forcing them to discard food. French cybersecurity authorities advised supermarkets to disconnect them from the internet. The attacks targeted Intermarché and Netto, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Monoprix, and E.Leclerc. The affected systems are said to be internet-facing and running outdated firmware. "The username is admin and the password changes every day automatically to.. the current date," security researcher Kevin Beaumont said. "Every single one is like this. You can just log in and change the temperature. Anybody can do it, easily scriptable." To make matters worse, the affected stores likely also failed to put the devices behind a VPN and create an allowlist of trusted IP addresses permitted to log in. "Two things would have changed the outcome," Pen Test Partners said. "Cyber hygiene would have prevented the access: take the controller off the public internet, put remote access behind a VPN and an IP allowlist, bring third-party kit onto the network in a controlled, owned and documented way rather than leaving it on a contractor's own connection, change known and default credentials, and patch to a current release." Multiple vulnerabilities have been disclosed in the affected models, with Claroty warning that the issues could be exploited to "defrost the food." Collabora RCE Flaw Exploited to Backdoor Nextcloud Servers — Threat actors are exploiting a critical command execution flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-110447 (CVSS score: 9.2), in the Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server app for Nextcloud to backdoor servers. It has been patched in version 26.4.303. The attacks involve issuing a malicious request to the app's "proxy.php" endpoint to trigger command injection and plant a PHP web shell with the end goal of conducting reconnaissance and searching for password databases, password manager artifacts, and cryptocurrency wallets. ‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. Fortra said it's tracking a 12-fold increase in emails using requests for quotation, project invitations, and procurement inquiries as phishing lures from October 2025 to September 2026. "These messages impersonate prospective buyers seeking pricing, availability, or project participation," Fortra said. "Their purpose is not to obtain a legitimate quote, but to persuade a recipient to access an attacker-controlled file-sharing, document-viewing, or procurement portal." A fake download site for the WatchGuard Mobile VPN with SSL ("watchguard-vpn[.]net") has been observed using a browser pop-up prompt to steal the victim's VPN server address, username, and password. As of October 13, the domain was offline. "In a unique twist, after collecting credentials twice (the first attempt gets rejected as 'incorrect' in a likely attempt to collect multiple credentials), the site then downloads the genuine, validly signed WatchGuard installer directly from WatchGuard's own content delivery network (CDN), meaning there is no malicious file for endpoint security tools to flag," Huntress said. "Meanwhile, unbeknownst to the victim, the threat actor now has access to their credentials, giving them access to victims' networks." A set of 42 malicious RubyGems packages has used typosquatting, brandjacking, and plausible utility names to target cryptocurrency and Web3 developers. The packages are designed to spawn a reverse shell and download a crypto theft kit capable of rerouting cryptocurrency transactions by replacing the destination address with an attacker-controlled wallet and harvesting wallet material, such as seed phrases and private keys. The names of some of the packages are: lightinng-invoice, cryoto-toolbox, etheremu.rb, bitcoin-rpc-lite, web3-sign-helper, and crypto-mnemonic-tools. The activity has been codenamed Ghost Dev by Open Source Malware. GreyNoise said it has observed a spike in scanning and exploitation attempts targeting Digital Video Recorders (DVRs) in Ukraine between September 21 and October 1, 2026. The majority of the activity attempts to exploit CVE-2021-36260, which allows unauthenticated command injection against unpatched Hikvision products. A series of email campaigns have been targeting the accommodation industry with fake guest complaints or reviews that deliver blockchain technology-abusing malware. "These emails appear to likely be a continuation of a prior series of predominantly Booking.com-spoofing emails that were seen delivering various remote access trojans (RAT) via ClickFix fake CAPTCHA websites," Cofense said. The activity leveraged the Ethereum and TON blockchains, a technique called EtherHiding, to deliver EtherRAT and TONResolver malware. As AI agents increasingly are being used to automate coding workflows, it increases the risk associated with credential exposure, Trellix warned. "Agents constantly take credentials out of the safe places your operating system keeps them, and put them somewhere far more exposed," Trellix said. "This happens as a normal side effect of everyday work. And even good security telemetry has a hard time distinguishing this from a developer doing their job -- or from an attacker who is already inside." MITRE released version 20 of its ATT&CK framework, adding entries that cover AI abuse, MFA bypass, and recent attacks on water utilities. This includes nine new Techniques and Sub-Techniques under the Enterprise domain for prompt injection, AI-enabled exfiltration, AI result poisoning, attacks on AI-assisted defenses, CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) evasion, and application-specific password theft. For Mobile, MITRE also un-deprecated a technique for delivering malicious apps outside official app stores, last included in v11. Fake AI tool campaigns that impersonate Claude, ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, and other AI brands are being used to plant infostealers on compromised systems using ClickFix lures. Some of the prominent targets include the U.S. and India. "The attacks share one trait: the employee performs the decisive step," ANY.RUN said. "They paste an 'install command,' run a convincing installer, or sign in to a fake window. That can put source code, cloud and AI API keys, active business sessions, ad accounts, and billing access at risk, turning a single user action into potential data exposure, account compromise, financial loss, or disruption to development and marketing operations." An official OpenAI skill, render-deploy, suffered from a first-of-its-kind supply-chain vulnerability which instructed production apps to send their tokens to an unregistered domain ("render-internal[.]com"). "It builds apps that trust a domain nobody owns, so any attacker could register it and start receiving tokens from real production apps," AIR Security said. "Vulnerable servers in the wild sent tokens to the domain, users are advised to update to the patched version of the skill." The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warned that scammers could exploit the 2026 U.S. midterm election to perpetrate financial fraud schemes. "As previously reported, scammers use the names, images, logos, and slogans of candidates to fraudulently solicit campaign contributions, sell merchandise that is never delivered, or steal personally identifiable information (PII) that can be used for other fraud," the FBI said. 1f2y31g.text: In February 2026, the operator of OnlyFake pleaded guilty in the United States for his role in a service that generated more than 10,000 fraudulent digital identity documents. Customers could create passports, driver’s licenses, Social Security cards, and documents from dozens of countries, then choose whether each appeared as a scan or a photograph of a physical ID. According to the U.S. Department of Justice, the documents allowed cybercriminals to conceal their identities, circumvent identity checks at banks and cryptocurrency exchanges, and launder money. The activity extends beyond fabricated documents. In underground communities monitored by Flare's platform, actors advertise manipulated photographs and videos, assistance with live identity verification, and accounts they claim have already passed identity checks. Each year, Flare collects hundreds of thousands of search results related to Know Your Client (KYC) services and the trade in verified accounts. Activity observed between March and September 2026 shows how these offerings are packaged and promoted across underground markets. What is KYC? It is the process that financial institutions use to establish a customer’s identity and assess the risk of providing services to them. Depending on the level of risk, they may validate the document, compare its photograph with a live image, confirm control of contact details, request information about the source of funds, and screen the customer against sanctions and politically exposed person lists. KYC continues after the account opening through transaction monitoring and additional verification when information changes or activity appears unusual. The Financial Action Task Force describes customer due diligence as identifying the customer, understanding the purpose of the relationship, and monitoring it over time. Is a Fake Identity Already Getting Past Your Checks? Underground sellers package forged documents, deepfakes, and live verification help to pass identity checks. Flare monitors criminal forums for exposed identities, stolen credentials, and active sessions, so you can invalidate access before it becomes account takeover or fraud. Free 2-Week Trial How KYC identity fraud works The steps and image below illustrate how actors assemble the elements used in KYC identity fraud: Identity data establishes the applicant’s claimed personal details. Documents are presented to substantiate those details. Photographs or videos associate the claimed identity with a face. Device and browser preparation makes the application session appear consistent with a legitimate customer’s. Live verification is attempted by a human operator or with synthetic media. Image explaining how KYC identity fraud works Building the identity package In March 2026, Flare observed a forum seller offering generated or edited identity and financial documents tailored to individual verification requests, including bank statements and other records that platforms may use to confirm an applicant’s address, income, or account ownership. The offer of complete KYC packages shows how sellers adapt several documents to the requirements of a particular platform or customer. Names, photographs, addresses, and other details must remain consistent across the application because a mismatch can trigger rejection or further review. This preparation creates the identity package later used during the facial or live verification stage. Screenshot from Flare's platform showing KYC services advertised on an underground forum.Sign up for the free trial to access if you aren’t already a customer. Bypassing live identity checks Many KYC systems compare the photograph on an identity document with a live image of the applicant. Some use passive liveness checks, which analyze a short camera recording for signs of a real person. Others use active checks that ask the applicant to turn their head, speak, blink, or read numbers shown on screen. To bypass these checks, actors advertise altered photographs and AI-generated videos based on the face shown in the identity document. Some tools claim to change the operator’s appearance during a live session, allowing the false face to follow instructions in real time by replacing the image coming from the physical camera with altered footage. Flare also observed advertisements for “human KYC,” in which a person completes facial or video verification using identity material prepared for the application. In one recruitment post, an actor sought someone who could use deepfake tools to alter the camera image during a live check and appear as the person named in the identity documents. Screenshot taken from Flare's platform showing the recruitment proposal in the forum.Sign up for the free trial to access if you aren’t already a customer. In another example, Flare researchers observed a threat actor advertising guidance for a live number-reading check. The applicant must respond to content presented during the session, thus the offered bypass requires coordination and adaptation rather than the submission of a prepared object. Support after the account is delivered Flare researchers observed sellers offering continued verification and account-recovery assistance after delivering a completed account, and the recruitment post above included help when a platform requested another identity check following handoff. When a later check requires the identity material or participant used during enrollment, the buyer may remain dependent on the seller, extending the original KYC service beyond the sale and helping preserve the appearance that the verified customer still controls the account. Detecting KYC abuse FinCEN has warned financial institutions that criminals are using deepfakes and fraudulent identity documents to bypass customer verification controls. Its alert recommends examining the complete application because differences between the applicant’s identity information, supporting records, facial images, and account activity may reveal that several elements were prepared by different people or tools. NIST recommends collecting identity documents and facial images directly during the verification session, checking whether they have been altered, and detecting software that replaces the footage from a physical camera. Unpredictable instructions, such as asking an applicant to make a particular movement or read changing numbers, can make prepared recordings harder to use, while information about the device can help determine whether the session comes from ordinary customer equipment. Applying these checks together gives organizations a better chance of detecting the combined use of false documents, deepfakes, and human operators described in underground KYC advertisements. Flare gives organizations additional visibility by monitoring criminal forums for exposed identities, stolen credentials, active login sessions, and threats connected to their organization. Security teams can use these alerts to identify affected accounts, invalidate exposed access, and investigate identity-related activity before it develops into account takeover or further fraud. 1kxc98.text: F5 has released out-of-band security patches to address multiple NGINX web server flaws, including three critical-severity vulnerabilities that can let attackers execute code on vulnerable systems. The three critical vulnerabilities were found in the ngx_http_v3_module (CVE-2026-15176 and CVE-2026-97205) and the NGINX map directive (CVE-2026-93479). Remote attackers without privileges can exploit them to launch denial-of-service (DoS) attacks or gain code execution on NGINX systems with non-default configurations. Successful exploitation causes a heap-based buffer overflow or use-after-free in the NGINX worker process, leading to crashes or a restart. However, attackers may also be able to "execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR." F5 released security patches for multiple NGINX software products affected by these two vulnerabilities, including NGINX Plus, NGINX Open Source, NGINX Ingress Controller, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and NGINX Instance Manager. Security teams and admins who can't immediately install these security patches can mitigate CVE-2026-15176 by not using the 'alias' directive in a location block or the $request_filename variable, and CVE-2026-97205 by disabling asynchronous file I/O (AIO) or Server Side Includes (SSI). CVE-2026-93479 can also be mitigated by using named captures instead of unnamed captures and limiting their use to the block with the regex match. While F5 has not yet flagged these security issues as exploited in the wild, cybercrime and nation-state threat groups have often exploited vulnerabilities in F5 products in recent years. For instance, attackers have targeted F5 security flaws to breach corporate networks, map internal servers, hijack devices, deploy data-wiping malware, and steal sensitive documents from victims worldwide. Since November 2021, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged eight F5 vulnerabilities as actively exploited, four of which have also been abused in ransomware attacks. One year ago, in October 2025, F5 also disclosed that state-sponsored threat actors breached its systems in August 2025 and stole source code and information on undisclosed BIG-IP security vulnerabilities. F5 is a Fortune 500 tech company that provides cybersecurity, application delivery networking (ADN), and other services to over 23,000 customers, including 80% of the Fortune Global 500 and 48 Fortune 50 companies.
