1vhzwlm.text: The threat actor behind the GhostAction supply chain attack has expanded beyond injecting malicious GitHub Actions workflows into compromised projects to phish open-source developers and deliver a stealer malware disguised within a fake font file. The latest evolution, detailed by OpenSourceMalware, signals that the attackers are actively refining their modus operandi in response to steps taken by GitHub to prevent the workflow from running. According to the threat intelligence platform, the threat actor registered the domain "my-github[.]com" and pointed it at "193.32.204[.]199," the same IP address that's used as an exfiltration endpoint for data harvested from running the malicious workflow. The domain was registered on October 9, 2026, 17 days after "my-gitlab[.]com" was registered. It's unclear if the latter code-hosting-themed domain is operated by the same threat actor. "It follows the same my-<code-host>.com naming pattern, making it a useful pivot, but current infrastructure does not directly connect it to GhostAction," security researcher Paul McCarty said. "They use different registrars, registrant records, Cloudflare nameserver pairs, IP addresses, ASNs, and DNS designs, and no shared certificate or account artifact has been recovered." Since then, the "my-github[.]com" domain has been used in a phishing email impersonating a GitHub security alert to target an open-source maintainer the same day it was registered. The message, sent from "noreply@my-github[.]com," warned of a new login to their GitHub account from Moscow, Russia, and instructed them to click on a link to secure their account. The deceptive page, per OpenSourceMalware, is said to have acted as a reverse proxy, harvesting the victim's password and two-factor authentication (2FA) code, and injected JavaScript that authorized an OAuth app with permissions to modify their workflows so as to facilitate a GhostAction-style attack. The fake login page also includes JavaScript to silently authorize a GitHub OAuth device flow with repo, workflow, and read:org scopes, granting it broad permissions to read/write repositories, modify Actions workflow files, and gain visibility into organization membership and related organizational data. The idea is the same as device code phishing, where the end goal is to obtain an access token from GitHub and exfiltrate it to "my-github[.]com" on TCP/8443. "The script receives a device code and user code, loads /login/device, extracts GitHub's forms from the returned HTML, and submits them automatically," McCarty explained. "It inserts the user code, locates an authorization form, adds authorize=1, and posts the approval through the victim's authenticated proxied session." "The victim does not need to type the device code or consciously approve the OAuth application. This kit goes further by automating the user-code and authorization steps through the reverse-proxied session." By stealing a repository-scoped OAuth token, it gives the attacker a reusable API credential. Furthermore, the permissions granted through the stealthy OAuth authorization are consistent with GhostAction's ability to enumerate repositories and inject malicious workflow files under ".github/workflows/." "The actor can now combine repository-scale automation with individual social engineering against people whose accounts provide access to projects, organizations, registries, and downstream users," OpenSourceMalware said. To make matters worse, the campaign has also been observed incorporating a second-stage component that persists on developer machines even after the malicious workflow has been removed. Specifically, the approach takes a leaf out of North Korea's playbook by committing three different files - A Microsoft Visual Studio Code (VS Code) tasks.json file with a "runOn: folderOpen" trigger that causes it to run automatically when the folder is opened in the application. A "public/fonts/fa-solid-400.woff2" file that contains a stealer payload designed to harvest AWS keys, PyPI tokens, npm tokens, Git logins, Kubernetes cluster credentials, SSH private keys, and AI provider credentials for Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini. The font file name is the same as one used in North Korea's PolinRider campaign from January 2026. A second GitHub Actions workflow that's activated if the infostealer never runs. This causes VS Code to auto-run the credential stealer, which, besides collecting data, installs a cron job that runs attacker-supplied code every five minutes. The collected data is sent to the same server over plain HTTP on port 8080. A total of 94 compromised repositories with the second-stage component have been identified. As for the second CI workflow, it's the same as the original malicious workflow, but with added credential formats to look for and a fallback that uploads findings to a secret GitHub gist if the POST fails. The second workflow goes by the following names - lint.yml ci-check.yml build-check.yml repo-health.yml audit.yml code-review.yml test-suite.yml cache-cleanup.yml OpenSourceMalware said the 94 repositories belong to 66 owners, out of which 15 have since been deleted, renamed, or made private. Of the still accessible repositories, most of them appear to have been largely abandoned, with one of them left untouched for more than nine years. Sixty-five of the 79 went without a commit for more than a year. "Stage 1 needs GitHub to run the workflow," OpenSourceMalware said. "On October 9, GitHub started preventing the malicious workflow from running, and the waves on October 10 and 12 extracted no secrets. Stage 2 adds a launcher that doesn't need a runner at all, and it arrived six days after the block. We can’t say the block caused it. We can say the operator moved to a place GitHub's controls don't reach." To mitigate the threat, developers should revoke GitHub access and tokens from a clean device, change their passwords, audit their repositories, rotate every credential the workflows can reach, and alert users who have cloned the repositories. "We don't know who the operator is, but their work suggests limited experience," Jenn Gile, co-founder of OpenSourceMalware, told The Hacker News. "The stealer's environment-variable filter misses most API keys, its home-directory search can time out and discard its own results, and a single IP handles exfiltration, phishing, and noisy internet scanning. That last mistake is why searching for the IP still finds infections."

28qf69.text: Microsoft has fixed a known issue that removed the Copilot Chat and Copilot buttons in the classic Outlook desktop mail client for some Windows users. As explained in an updated support document, affected users with the Copilot Chat (Basic) license or a Microsoft 365 Copilot (Premium) account no longer saw Copilot buttons in the side navigation and above the ribbon. Those impacted by this experienced one or more of the following issues: The Copilot button missing from the top-right area above the ribbon. The Copilot icon missing from the left app bar or More Apps area in classic Outlook. In Add Apps, Copilot may appear as an available app, but selecting Open does nothing. Adding Copilot through ribbon customization may show the command as unavailable or grayed out. Copilot remains available from other entry points, such as Outlook on the web or the Microsoft Copilot standalone app or web experience. Microsoft first announced in June that it had fixed the bug with a service change, but last month it said it had started investigating again after recent updates caused it to resurface. Now, Microsoft says it has finally resolved this classic Outlook issue, blaming it on a bug that prevented Outlook from retrieving some account information from the user's Outlook profile. "We fixed an issue in classic Outlook that could cause the Copilot entry point to be missing from the navigation pane when required account information could not be retrieved from the user’s Outlook profile. The Copilot button might be missing for several different reasons, including licensing, Microsoft 365 app configuration, update channel, privacy settings, or other environmental factors," an update to the original support document reads. "Because the missing button is a symptom that can have multiple underlying causes, we recommend following the guidance in Copilot troubleshooters and How to find and enable missing Copilot button in Microsoft 365 apps to identify and resolve the issue." Microsoft also shared a temporary workaround for those still affected by this known issue, which requires enabling the "Show Apps in Outlook" option in classic Outlook settings by selecting the File tab, then going to Options > Advanced and checking the "Show Apps in Outlook" box under "Outlook panes." Affected users can also use the new Outlook email client or Outlook Web Access (OWA), which are not affected by this bug, or create a new Outlook profile. Since the start of the year, Microsoft has also resolved known issues that prevented some classic Outlook users from sending emails via Outlook.com and rendered the classic Outlook client unusable when enabling the Microsoft Teams Meeting Add-in. 194m92b.text: In Salesforce Agentforce, the recommended way to make an agent respond to events is a Flow: a record is created or a case is updated, and the Flow passes data into the agent's prompt. Separately, Email-to-Case and Web-to-Case turn inbound customer messages into case records; it is how airlines and hotels run support intake. Both are standard, documented, as-designed features. Chained together, they produce this path: public internet → email → case record → agent prompt → agent action → case comment → outbound reply An unauthenticated outsider now has a route into an internal agent's instructions, and the agent's reply leaves through the same door. Nothing was misconfigured. The finding, documented by researchers in August 2026, is a clean example of how agents that arrive inside existing platforms fail: through the application around them, not the model inside them. The risk is in the application, and the application is the thing nobody re-reviewed Which intake features are enabled, which triggers fire, which objects are exposed to guest users, which automation passes untrusted data where, and which model version the agent is quietly calling underneath: these are the variables that decide whether the Agentforce chain is a support-queue nuisance or a data exposure. A vendor risk review performed once at procurement sees none of them, because the agent did not exist at procurement. A prompt filter watching the agent's inputs does not know that a particular input originated from a stranger, because prompt filters do not understand Email-to-Case. Securing an inherited agent therefore means understanding its host application at the depth its own admins do. That depth is the one thing a questionnaire and a scanner both lack. The City-Forum campaign, an active worldwide data-theft operation against Salesforce and ServiceNow instances running since March 2025, was found in exactly this territory: the gap between platform features and the configurations enterprises actually run. Builders are multiplying, and some of them are agents The platforms have made agent creation as accessible as making a slide deck. Marketing operations builds an agent to pull pipeline reports. Finance builds one to reconcile invoices. Each rides its creator's permissions, because that is what makes it useful. Shadow AI was an employee pasting data into a chatbot. Shadow agents are that employee's access, running unattended, multiplied across everything they were ever granted. Increasingly, agents also build agents. A coding agent tagged into a chat channel can scaffold and deploy another agent as easily as it opens a pull request; an orchestration platform spins up sub-agents to divide a task, each with its own connections and none with its own review. Any governance model that assumes a human requested each agent is quietly obsolete. Why governance keeps producing a document Ask a large enterprise about agent governance and the answer is usually a document: an acceptable-use policy, a monthly committee, a set of principles nobody disputes and nothing enforces. Ask the operational question, how many agents are running right now, what can they reach, and who owns each one, and the document does not know. The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 now describes the sharpest version of this gap under its "No Governance" category: a skill deployed and managed inside a third-party platform is unreachable by external scanners (OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 whitepaper, ast10-top10-whitepaper-2, published at owasp.github.io). The tools an enterprise points at the problem from outside cannot see inside the venues where most agents live. Governance fails most often because the rules get written before the security team can see the things the rules apply to. The stack, bottom-up, with a test for each layer The working order is bottom-up, and each layer is the precondition for the one above it. A practical way to check whether a program is real is to apply an operational test at each level. Layer What it has to produce The operational test Discovery A continuously refreshed population across app configs, OAuth grants, network, endpoint, email metadata, and browser Is the discovered count several multiples of the list IT keeps? If not, discovery isn't reaching where agents live. Posture Every platform's agent-relevant settings, measured against how they should be configured Can the team list the intake features and guest-user exposures wired to agent triggers on its top three platforms? Identity and ownership An identity and a named owner per agent, with a lifecycle Pick an agent at random. Does a human raise a hand within a day when asked "whose is this?" Usage Who is building what, through which surface, with what data Is there a sanctioned path that ships a business team's agent with secure defaults, or only a block? Agent controls Least privilege against observed need, approval and quarantine for new agents, risk tiering that reflects each agent's full context Does the same finding on a sandboxed dev agent and a customer-facing one show different severities? Runtime Live inspection and intervention Is it fed by the five layers above, or deployed first and enforcing blind? The cost of paper compliance The EU AI Act's penalties carry GDPR-level weight: up to €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover for prohibited practices, up to €15 million or 3% for other violations. Every framework converging on it assumes the stack above exists. GDPR already showed what happens when it does not. British Airways (£20 million) and Marriott (£18.4 million) were not fined for having imperfect policies. Everyone has imperfect policies. They were fined because compliance existed on paper and could not be evidenced operationally when regulators asked. A governance practice built bottom-up generates that evidence as a byproduct: the inventory, the owners, the configurations, the review history. Some platforms are designed to produce exactly that record. One leading example is Reco, which discovers agents across multiple vantage points, including the ones that never touch SSO, and assigns each a risk profile before any policy can be applied to it. The Agentforce chain at the top of this article is not an exploit. It is a configuration, and configurations are governable, provided someone can see them. Chapters 1 to 3 of Into the Expanse cover the shift, the three launch vectors, and the governance practice in full: https://www.reco.ai/agent-ecosystem-security

15qjr4s.text: A fake Web3 accelerator has been observed pushing information stealers and backdoors to Windows and macOS systems using malicious npm packages under the pretext of offering free artificial intelligence (AI) credits for Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini, coding tools, and security audits. "The tools delivered information-stealing malware and backdoors for macOS and Windows machines," Elastic Security Labs researchers Jia Yu Chan and Daniel Stepanic said. "The operation also repackaged a legitimate coding agent to send model requests through attacker-controlled services, while its audit tools generated fabricated security findings." The scheme poses as a Web3 venture capital accelerator named Apex Accelerator to target cryptocurrency startups and founders. It's being tracked under the moniker REF8801. The names of the npm packages, each of which targets both Windows and macOS machines, are listed below - @apexacc/cli (Apex Copilot CLI — AI advisor for Web3 founders) - @apexacc/audit (Web3 Security Scanner — 18 tools for DYOR and smart contract auditing) While both the packages and their associated GitHub repositories are no longer accessible, "@apexacc/cli" was advertised as an "AI advisor for Web3 founders" that's powered by Claude Fable 5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash. "@apexacc/audit," on the other hand, claimed to be a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposing 18 security tools for scanning tokens, wallets, and smart contracts. Both packages were published by an npm user named "apexaccelerator" and linked to a GitHub account called "apexaccs" and an entity referred to as the Apex Foundation. Interestingly, the campaign itself is not new. In late July 2026, SafeDep detailed three other npm packages linked to the same operation that were found distributing a macOS stealer belonging to the Atomic Stealer (aka AMOS) family - @apexfdn/apex @copilot-mcp/apex, which features the same package description as "@apexacc/cli" @apexfdn/copilot-mcp, which claims to be an Apex Copilot and MCP server for "portfolio diligence and operator tools" Artifacts captured by Socket show that the Apex Foundation has been linked to at least two distinct domains since April 2026 apexaccs[.]org apexfdn[.]xyz According to Internet Archive snapshots dating back to March 19, 2026, the foundation states: "The Apex Foundation offers $235,000 investments, grants, and partnerships, and connects projects with VCs, angels, and private equity if they don't meet our criteria." Posts shared on X show the accelerator approaching developers of cryptocurrency wallets and market intelligence tools for traders with offers of direct investment and instructions to run their due diligence tool ("@apexacc/cli"). In the case of the latter, the npm package has been found to drop an encrypted malware loader disguised as an Apple app ("com.apple.system.loader"). "The group also sought to build credibility through its presence at TOKEN2049 in Singapore and other in-person events it has hosted in the past," Elastic said. "The group attempts to manufacture legitimacy by appearing at widely attended conferences, indirectly lending credibility to the project." Once installed, neither of the npm packages provides the promised functionality. The 18 security tools part of the @apexacc/audit package generate fabricated findings, while @apexacc/cli's scoring test returns an unsupported assessment of a fictitious project. Instead, their primary responsibility is to propagate a macOS backdoor called CloudSyncD and a custom Windows information stealer that exfiltrates data through Telegram. The platform-specific executables are retrieved from the projects' GitHub releases. Both packages implement a distinct verification path for Windows and macOS by sending an HTTP POST request to "win32" or "darwin" to "vrf.apexaccs[.]org/api/v1/vrf" to initiate the appropriate next stage. The Windows and macOS infection chains are as follows - Windows - The malware retrieves a Base64-encoded PowerShell command, which reaches out to another endpoint ("0auth-chromium[.]com/APIService") to fetch a second PowerShell script ("drop.ps1") that downloads an executable ("bludness.exe") from "ehegisnightmare[.]icu" and launches it in a hidden window. The PyInstaller executable is a Python loader that checks if it already has administrator privileges and, if so, downloads the next stage from "ehegisnightmare[.]icu," saves it as "%TEMP%\exegis.exe," and launches it. If not, it attempts to bypass User Account Control (UAC) using UACME's ucmDebugObjectMethod(). The "exegis.exe" binary is another PyInstaller executable that collects system metadata, running processes, and performs anti-virtual-machine (anti-VM) checks before decrypting and launching a bundled loader as "%TEMP%\updater_loader.exe." The Golang executable patches Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) and Event Tracing for Windows (ETW), unhooks "ntdll.dll" to blind endpoint security tools, and loads the next-stage shellcode into its own memory. The shellcode is a native information stealer that examines for signs of a prior infection and then harvests system information, clipboard text, process listings, Wi-Fi profile names, screenshots, and data from wallets, browser extensions, messengers, remote-access and file transfer protocol (FTP) applications, virtual private network (VPN) clients, browsers (Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and Yandex), and game clients. The stealer can also bypass Chrome's app-bound encryption (ABE) protections to extract saved passwords, session cookies, browsing history, download records, and profile metadata. The collected data is exfiltrated through Telegram. macOS - The malware downloads a remotely hosted bash script and executes it on the machine. The shell script downloads a GZIP-compressed archive from "verify.apexfdn[.]xyz/unix/," saves it as "package.tar.gz" in a temporary directory, and extracts its contents. The archive contains a dropper for CloudSyncD, which first phishes the victim's system login password using a fake authorization prompt and then uses it to launch an embedded payload with sudo privileges. The payload performs host discovery, collects hardware and operating-system details, and then contacts an external server ("ccmihr[.]com") to transmit the data and receive further tasks that allow the malware to download and run additional payloads. It's worth noting that CloudSyncD was first documented by Jamf Threat Labs late last month, detailing its propagation via a fake Zoom installer. The malware was detected in the wild in mid-September 2026. "Its behaviors illustrate how macOS malware continues to move toward native implementations, string protection, and execution paths that attempt to avoid writing payloads to disk, while still depending on the oldest technique available: asking the user for their password," Jamf said. Besides deploying a stealer and backdoor depending upon the infected operating system, the packages are capable of intercepting and redirecting OpenRouter large language model (LLM) traffic, as well as registering an MCP server under their control in the victim's agent configuration. "These changes allow the attacker-controlled API to receive the prompts, conversation history, code snippets, and tool outputs included in the agent's LLM requests," Elastic researchers explained. "The attacker's MCP server can also supply instructions that are added to the agent's prompt, along with tool names, descriptions, and accepted inputs that help the model decide which tools to invoke and how to use them. Together, these mechanisms give the attacker visibility into the submitted data and a way to influence the agent's subsequent actions."

7rfpnf.text: Microsoft has confirmed that this month's Windows Server security updates are causing OWA sign-in and mail delivery issues on some Exchange Server systems. In a new Windows release health dashboard update over the weekend, Microsoft said users may have trouble accessing email or signing in to Outlook after installing the latest updates on systems running Windows Server 2019 and later. In some cases, affected customers are also reportedly seeing Exchange Server OWA failing with a "MapiExceptionMdbOffline: Unable to make connection to the server. (hr=0x80004005, ec=1142)" error and Event ID 1006 in the application log. "After installing the October 2026 Windows security update [..], some on-premises Exchange servers might experience issues accessing or sending email. Users might be unable to sign in to Outlook on the web (OWA), or email messages sent from Outlook might remain in the Outbox and not be delivered. Additionally, Exchange might experience issues accessing mailboxes during mailbox replication," it said. "The October 2026 update introduced a default limit on the amount of memory used by Endpoint Mapper when handling Endpoint Lookup calls. For workloads such as Exchange Server, the default limit of 512 simultaneous Endpoint Lookup calls might not be sufficient under heavy load. Administrators can use this registry setting to increase the maximum number of simultaneous Endpoint Lookup calls, which increases the amount of memory that Endpoint Mapper can use." However, Microsoft says these known issues aren't linked to the October 2026 Exchange server security updates and urges customers not to uninstall them. "Issues reported are not related to installation of October 2026 security updates for Exchange Server. This is not a 'known issue' related to October 2026 Exchange update. Any version of Exchange that runs on impacted versions of Windows could be impacted," Microsoft added in a separate blog describing the issues. "Not all Exchange servers will be impacted by installation of those updates equally; the severity and speed of impact varies based on Exchange server load. Some servers might never see a problem." While it works on a fix, Microsoft also shared a temporary workaround that should resolve these issues by modifying a registry key on affected Exchange Server systems. To do that, you have to run the following command from an elevated Command Prompt on the Exchange Server and then reboot the device: reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Rpc" /v EpmapSavedContextCap /t REG_DWORD /d 65536 /f After the system restarts, customers should monitor the Exchange environment and raise the Endpoint Mapper memory limit if it reoccurs. In July. Microsoft also announced that it will stop shipping extended security updates for Exchange 2016 and 2019 this month after a 6-month extension announced in April 2026 to the original Extended Security Update (ESU) program. 1gxrqwp.text: A flaw in Broadcom's Wi-Fi setup software lets an attacker within radio range run code as root on Broadcom-based routers, without the network password or any pairing step, security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed on October 16. He showed the attack working against home gateways supplied by three Belgian internet providers, in one case reading the Wi-Fi password off the device and in another opening a remote shell over the air. No CVE has been assigned to the flaw, and no fix has been deployed to the affected routers, Kaiser says. The flaw is in Broadcom's version of Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), the feature that lets a device join a Wi-Fi network without the password being typed in. Broadcom's code mishandles the reassembly of fragmented WPS setup messages, so an attacker in range can send crafted messages that corrupt the router's memory. From there, Kaiser built two things: a way to read memory back off the device, and a way to run his own code on it. Against an Orange Belgium gateway, the Askey TCG3000 read the Wi-Fi password (the PSK) from the router's stored settings, sent it back over the air, and then joined the network with it. Against a Proximus gateway, the Sagemcom-built BBOX3V+, the exploit opened a reverse shell, a remote command line, carried over Wi-Fi frames, so no outside server was needed. Both ran without any login, and the attack works at a distance, not only up close, Kaiser says. He reports no real-world attacks using the flaw. The working exploits are his own. What's Affected Broadcom's WPS code is embedded in routers and access points from dozens of vendors, and Kaiser estimates that millions of devices worldwide are affected. The vulnerable chips fall into two families: older eCos-based models (the BCM3380, BCM3383 and BCM33834), where he found no usable fix and calls the bug a permanent "forever day," meaning a flaw that will never be patched on those devices, and newer Linux-based models (the BCM3390, BCM65xx and BCM68xx), which could be fixed if their makers switch Wi-Fi software. In Belgium, Kaiser found the flaw present and exploitable on gateways from three of the four big providers: Proximus, Orange Belgium and VOO. A fourth, Telenet, may be affected too, but he could not test one. A wider list he published, ranging from Cisco small-business access points to Huawei and ARRIS routers, mixes confirmed and unconfirmed entries, and some rest on an automated check that only flags a device as "likely vulnerable." The Belgian per-provider counts, he says, run into the hundreds of thousands of gateways, but are rough estimates. Why There's No Patch, and No CVE The flaw is old. Kaiser traces the code back to at least 2010 and says Broadcom shipped an incomplete fix in 2018, then told customers to switch to a different Wi-Fi software package, called hostapd, rather than relying on the fix. On the older eCos chips, he says, no working fix was ever shipped, which is why he calls it a forever day. No CVE, the tracking identifier that lets defenders and vendors follow a flaw, has been assigned to it. Kaiser says Broadcom told him it has known about the bug since 2018 and had heard about it from others, but would not register a CVE or say anything publicly, which he believes is why so many device makers never patched. When he took the case to the CERT Coordination Center, it was closed the same day, because Broadcom itself holds the authority to assign CVEs for its products and would not do so. The Hacker News found no CVE for the flaw as of October 19. What Defenders Can Do There is no patch to install, and no setting Kaiser points to that blocks the attack over the air. What he provides instead is a way to find affected gear: YARA rules that spot the vulnerable code in extracted firmware, and a script that listens to a live access point and reports whether it looks vulnerable. Both are triage aids, he notes: a patched device can still match the rules, so a hit is a reason to check further, not a confirmed finding. For gear that will never be fixed, replacement is the practical option. Kaiser frames the bug as well suited to attackers who reach a target over nearby Wi-Fi rather than the internet, a technique Russian state hackers have used to breach networks from across the street.

ffnn48.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 19, 2026Data Breach / Artificial Intelligence An intruder reached a legacy system at OpenCode on the night of October 16 and may have exposed the third-party AI provider keys that users had saved in OpenCode Console, the company said. Console is OpenCode's optional hosted service: a workspace saves its own OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google key there, and Console uses that key to call the provider so team members can use the models without ever seeing the key. The affected group is 1.4% of Console users, all of whom have an outside provider linked, and OpenCode has told them via email to revoke those keys with each provider and replace them. The email went out on the morning of October 17 under the subject line "Action Required: Potential provider key breach." Anyone who did not get one was not affected, OpenCode said in a post on X later that day. The keys at risk are the ones pasted into Console. The OpenCode command-line and desktop apps keep provider keys added on the machine in a SQLite database there. The breach involves "the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself," co-founder Dax Raad wrote in a reply on X, and those keys "never come to us." A provider key is a bearer credential: whoever holds a copy can run billable requests against the owner's account until the provider revokes it. Deleting the key from Console does not revoke it, and a Console budget cannot cap that use either, because Console only sees requests that pass through its own gateway. For a key that was saved in a Console workspace, OpenCode's email and the providers' own guidance give these steps: Revoke the key in the provider's own dashboard and create a new one, following the instructions from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google. Update every application and script that used the old key. Review usage and billing at the provider for requests you did not make, going back at least to October 16. OpenCode has not said when the unauthorized access began. Set a spend limit or alert at the provider and give each tool its own key, so a copied key does less damage and its use is easier to trace. Some users say they have already paid for usage they did not run. Dealroom reported that Colin Parsons wrote on X that his OpenAI key had been used for $281 and his Anthropic key for $168, and that Preston Zeller put his losses at $1,700. Notebookcheck reported a Reddit user's claim of $400 of unauthorized usage on an Anthropic account, and another's of about €200 of Google usage, with the project then suspended. Those are the users' own accounts. OpenCode's own wording is that the keys "may have been exposed," and it has not said that any key was copied or used. OpenCode's October 17 post also called the incident ongoing, said the company was working with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to fix it, and described the breach as "related to a large-scale distillation attack." The company has not named anyone or said how the two connect, what the legacy system was, how it was reached, how many keys it held, or how many users 1.4% represents. Distillation is the term AI model providers use for campaigns that pull a model's answers in huge numbers to train a rival model. Anthropic said in September that the labs behind such campaigns reach its models through networks of fake accounts created with stolen credit cards, login credentials and harvested API keys. A stolen key has other uses too: criminal markets resell AI tokens and keys and use them to run up bills. Attackers were still trying to get into OpenCode's systems on October 18, Raad wrote on X: they had been "non stop trying to attack our systems for the past 48 hours," and "a side effect is everything is getting hardened."

un4d11.text: Hackers are exploiting an OS command-injection vulnerability in the SiteGuard Server Edition web application firewall (WAF), allowing them to execute commands with root or SYSTEM privileges on affected machines. The security issue is tracked as CVE-2026-106931 and affects the statistics feature in host-based WAF instances, which is enabled by default. SiteGuard is a leading Japanese WAF vendor that claims to protect more than 1.5 million websites. Based on WordPress.org statistics, the product is active on 500,000 sites. According to the vendor’s bulletin and a warning from Japan's CERT agency, CVE-2026-106931 has critical severity and is currently being exploited in the wild. “An OS command injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-106931) has been found in the statistics function of SiteGuard Server Edition. Abuse has already been confirmed,” reads SiteGuard’s alert. The attacker’s identity, the victims, the scale of the attacks, and the methods used remain unclear, as neither security advisory provides these details. According to the vendor, the following versions of the product are vulnerable to CVE-2026-106931: SiteGuard Server Edition for Apache httpd, Nginx, and IIS (excluding FreeBSD) versions 2.20 and later, before 8.00 Update 5. SiteGuard Server Edition for Apache httpd and Nginx on FreeBSD versions 2.20 and later, before 7.00 Update 6. Successful exploitation is possible in the above versions if the statistics function is active. IIS editions 3.10 through 4.00 Update 4, inclusive, are not affected, JPCERT/CC notes. For installations that cannot be upgraded, the vendor offers a patch that replaces files used in statistics processing, including for end-of-life versions. The vendor warns that remediation may erase attack traces, and recommends that administrators preserve evidence before updating or patching. To do this, administrators are instructed to download and retain “Diagnostic information” from the web management interface (Web management screen ‐>Diagnostic information‐> Download diagnostic information) The vendor said customers with direct support contacts were notified of the flaw earlier, on September 29. shs9gu.text: ConnectWise on Saturday said it has disabled seven ConnectWise application identities as it continues its investigation into an incident in which unknown threat actors obtained unauthorized access to the application identities and compromised Microsoft 365 tenants. The disabled identities are listed below - ConnectWise Cloud Backup - 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae ConnectWise Cloud Management - 2399d300-6fca-4e6a-a686-399fefe75b83 ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams - 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640 ConnectWise Cloud Management - Exchange Online - b78f6a77-d4e5-46fb-87e5-d1648bd02519 ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Graph - 0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827 ConnectWise Cloud Management - Partner Center - 412dcf96-176d-4b3a-a1b0-4981ad66971e ConnectWise Cloud Management - SharePoint Online - b2b55f5b-7758-4719-8d8f-88ae172e6bdb The IT management software provider said it took the action on October 17, 2026, at 07:00 UTC, adding it has also suspended Cloud Backup service by revoking certificates used for affected application connections across all users. "Disabling the affected connections prevents new authentication through those connections; it does not reverse changes previously made inside a tenant," it said. "The affected shared Cloud Backup credentials are no longer valid. Previously issued access tokens may remain usable until they expire or are otherwise invalidated. Any unauthorized credentials, permissions, or other access established through separate identities require additional review and remediation." ConnectWise also noted that scheduled backups are not running, and access to affected backup archives and restoration capabilities remains unavailable. However, it emphasized that existing archives remain encrypted, isolated, and preserved, and that there is no evidence they were breached or accessed by the attackers. Out of an abundance of caution, the company said it has temporarily taken SaaS Security and Cloud Management offline while it completes its review of the incident. Furthermore, the company revealed that it identified the issue on October 14, 2026, through its "advanced cybersecurity monitoring and diligence," prompting it to activate internal and external incident investigation and response actions. "Since implementing these mitigations, we have not observed successful threat activity in the environments we monitor," it said. "This finding does not establish the status of downstream customer environments, which, by design, we cannot directly observe." At this stage, it's unclear if a product vulnerability contributed to the compromise of the application identities. The exact credential-exposure mechanism is the subject of an ongoing analysis, ConnectWise added. The attack is particularly dangerous as it allows an attacker to abuse the application's credentials to access customers' Microsoft 365 environments without having to steal each customer's password individually. By using the stolen application credential to authenticate as that application, the attacker can request access tokens from Microsoft Entra ID based on the application's existing permissions. Depending on the permissions assigned to the application, this could enable the attacker to potentially access other Microsoft services, including mailboxes, SharePoint documents, Teams messages, and directory information. With ConnectWise's applications operating with extensive permissions to perform backups and management tasks, the theft of the credential allows the threat actor to authenticate as the application itself and expand their access by adding it to the Global Administrator role, adding client secrets to other trusted applications in the tenant, and creating new applications and granting them permissions. By doing so, the client secrets offer a way to authenticate as that application and establish persistence, providing an alternative means to regain access to the compromised environment even if the original compromised credential is later revoked. Second, Targeted Wave of Attempts Observed "We last observed malicious sign-ins from the original address on October 15 at 08:45 UTC, with targeted, manual activity continuing until about 14:20 UTC that day," Jon Semon, Principal Security Operations Analyst at Huntress, told The Hacker News. "ConnectWise has said access to Cloud Backup is shut off, and if so, activity through that service should have stopped. However, if the threat actor was able to add credentials to applications in Microsoft tenants, those credentials would let them keep access and act as the application." Huntress said it has not identified new malicious activity since October 15, but there is no evidence that the stoppage was the result of public disclosure. "We have high confidence the threat actor also targeted the ConnectWise Cloud Management apps for Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, and SharePoint, and we have confirmed abuse of the Teams app in one tenant," Semon said. "Those apps do not appear to have been disabled by ConnectWise, so additional activity could come from them, and we are actively investigating." As of late Saturday, Huntress said it identified a "second, targeted wave of attempts" from the IP address "144.172.64[.]128" on October 15. These efforts, which singled out a narrow scope of 16 tenants, were unsuccessful. The tenants are in the policy, national security, trade, and critical mineral sectors. "For the new target set, the first sweep targeted Graph tokens from the SkyKick app and occurred on October 15 between 09:25:04 and 12:35:50 UTC," Huntress said. "The second sweep hit the same tenants on the same date, between 13:54:39 and 14:20:24 UTC. This sweep appeared to be manual and targeted Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Teams, Azure Resource Manager, Entra, and the Office 365 Management APIs." In all, the managed security service provider has identified almost 1,000 Entra tenants with sign-in activity from the IP address associated with the unauthorized activity from the IP address in question, out of which 300 succeeded. Despite the successful sign-in, the absence of a service principal in some tenants is said to have prevented the threat actor from gaining access to those tenants. Partners are advised to take the following actions - Review both their own Microsoft 365 tenant and each managed customer tenant, including environments with dormant SkyKick connections. Verify the status of the listed application connections and keep affected applications disabled until further notice. Review sign-ins across identities from October 13, 2026, through the current time, specifically for activity originating from the IP address "144.172.64[.]128." Preserve available sign-in and audit records before initiating containment steps. Review application and user authentication, application credentials and federation trusts, directory roles, owners, consent grants, and recent policy changes. Check for unauthorized mailbox forwarding, inbox or transport rules, and delegated mailbox access. Investigate any other identities changed or used during suspicious activity. "Several Entra controls limit the damage if an application credential is stolen," Huntress said. "Application management policies can restrict or block client secrets on app registrations and cap credential lifetimes. Limiting who holds the Application Administrator and Cloud Application Administrator roles reduces who can add credentials to applications." "Conditional Access for workload identities, which needs additional licensing, can restrict where an application is allowed to sign in from, and Microsoft Entra ID Protection can flag risky service principals. None of these replace reviewing credentials, but they make a planted secret harder to use or easier to spot."

9lq3kc.text: ConnectWise has shut down customer access to its Cloud Backup service (formerly SkyKick Cloud Backup) after hackers accessed application identities and compromised Microsoft 365 tenants. Reports of the malicious activity began emerging on Friday, with administrators observing unauthorized access to client data in Microsoft 365 tenants due to a potential “SkyKick/CW breach.” Later on the same day, managed cybersecurity and threat detection platform Huntress confirmed the worries, saying that it had identified at least 162 compromised tenants in its environment. In a post today, Microsoft also confirmed malicious activity involving ConnectWise’s Cloud Backup service, saying it identified unauthorized authentication attempts from an IP address on October 15. ConnectWise’s cloud backup solutions provide backup and recovery services that help managed service providers (MSPs) and IT teams protect and restore customer data, such as emails and files, in cloud environments including Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace. For Microsoft 365 backups, the service relies on permissions granted through Microsoft Entra ID. An application identity known as a “service principal” represents the software in a customer’s tenant and enables it to access resources according to the permissions granted. Microsoft 365 tenant breaches In a security advisory, ConnectWise said that it “recently identified unauthorized access to application identities within the ConnectWise Cloud Backup environment” and shut down application access for its partners and clients. “We have no indicators to date that Cloud Backup partner backup data has been compromised. The existing cloud backup archive is not impacted by this service interruption and will be accessible once services are restored,” ConnectWise says. However, the company has launched an investigation and is engaged in remediation efforts. Based on reports from Microsoft, Huntress, and administrators, the malicious activity started at least on October 15 from a single IP address: 144.172.64[.]128. One user on Reddit said that they received a notification from the Microsoft Privileged Identity Management (PIM) service on October 15 alerting of a SkyKick service principal assigning itself the role of Exchange Administrator, despite not using the app in years. Nevertheless, some of the reported IDs for the offensive SkyKick match those provided by Huntress, Microsoft, and Todyl - a cybersecurity platform primarily for MSPs and IT professionals. According to Todyl researchers, the attacker authenticated directly to Microsoft 365 as the backup application using its secret, gaining the permissions customers had already granted it. The sign-in requests were performed by an automated script, and since they did not involve a user login, protections such as multi-factor authentication (MFA) were ineffective. “Because the application already held broad, previously granted permissions in each tenant, those sign-ins gave the attacker the technical ability to read and write mail and attachments, OneDrive and SharePoint files, and Teams chats,” Todyl said. In the analyzed intrusions on nine tenants, Todyl researchers identified only sign-in activity and did not find evidence that the threat actor “created accounts, added permissions, changed passwords, or established persistence in any tenant through the backup app.” Reconnaissance and persistence attempts However, Huntress saw on nearly 50 tenants it monitors that service principals for “ConnectWise’s Cloud Management apps (Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, and Microsoft Graph) assigned themselves directory roles, mostly Exchange Administrator.” In one tenant, Huntress researchers also observed that the attacker established persistence, the operation taking around five minutes. During the activity, Cloud Management - MS Teams (24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640) granted itself a Global Administrator role and added credentials to an MSP management tool and to Huntress’s own application. Microsoft also observed persistence activity via a backdoor after successful service principal authentication, followed by “Microsoft Graph API reconnaissance and attempts to add additional credentials.” It should be noted that all three cybersecurity companies tracked the malicious company to the same 144.172.64[.]128 IP address. Microsoft Threat Intelligence characterized the incident as an active supply-chain attack, assessing that the attacker likely abused existing permissions, including Directory.ReadWrite.All. Indicators and tenant checks Huntress identified the legitimate Cloud Backup application ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae used in the attacks. Its investigation also linked the attacker IP address to scripted sign-in attempts on October 13 and 14, with the user agent curl/7.88.1. Based on current evidence, there are at least three user agents linked to the malicious Cloud Backup service activity: python-urllib/3.12, python-requests/2.31, python-requests/2.34.2.​ ConnectWise recommends that administrators check the service principal sign-ins in Entra, filter by the Cloud Backup application ID, and examine unexpected source addresses. Microsoft also recommends reviewing application credential changes, OAuth grants, and related Graph activity. Huntress advises administrators to disable the implicated ConnectWise applications, as well as check application credentials for unauthorized additions and review other Cloud Management integrations. The company notes that older tenants may list Cloud Management apps under ‘SkyKick Cloud Manager’. The company provides an extended list of application IDs for administrators to look for: ConnectWise Cloud Backup (506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae) ​ConnectWise Cloud Management (2399d300-6fca-4e6a-a686-399fefe75b83) ​ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams (24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640) ​ConnectWise Cloud Management - Exchange Online (b78f6a77-d4e5-46fb-87e5-d1648bd02519) ​ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Graph (0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827) ​ConnectWise Cloud Management - Partner Center (412dcf96-176d-4b3a-a1b0-4981ad66971e) ​ConnectWise Cloud Management - SharePoint Online (b2b55f5b-7758-4719-8d8f-88ae172e6bdb) The vendor’s shutdown does not remove credentials already planted in customer tenants. Huntress says that admins should review secrets and certificates across all applications for unauthorized additions since October 13 and removing those entries. Todyl warns that disabling an application stops new tokens from being issued, but existing tokens remain valid until they expire, and revoking user sessions does not end application-based access. ConnectWise announced the backup service interruption at 05:01 UTC on October 17 but did not provide a timeline for restoring the connection. The company did not report any evidence that stored backups were compromised and said existing archives would be accessible when reservices are restored. At the time of publishing the victim count and the extent of data theft remains unclear, as well as the method the attacker used to obtain vendor credentials. 17uz5p7.text: Drupal has patched two critical vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to execute code remotely on websites running any supported version of the content management system. The security issues impact the software core's Field UI module and the contributed Entity List module. Drupal issued an advance warning at the beginning of the week, urging administrators to apply updates promptly because attackers could develop exploits shortly after the vulnerabilities’ disclosure. “The Drupal Security Team urges you to reserve time for core updates at that time because exploits might be developed within hours or days,” the project's security team warned. “We recommend updating to the latest supported patch (bugfix) release for your site's version of Drupal before October 14, so that you can address any other upgrade issues before the security window.” Drupal is a free, open-source content management system used to build and manage websites, particularly popular among government agencies, universities, and non-profit organizations. According to the project’s website, more than one million websites run on Drupal. Earlier this week, the open-source project disclosed the two details, noting that "all currently supported versions of Drupal core are affected." CVE-2026-108097: A remote code execution vulnerability in Drupal core’s Field UI module that could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected servers. CVE-2026-108099: A flaw in Entity List, a contributed module for creating entity lists without Views, that could enable remote code execution. The security advisory for CVE-2026-108097 notes that the flaw cannot be exploited using Drupal core alone, but contributed modules can provide multiple exploitation paths, including at least one that requires no authentication. Additionally, custom code may also expose the vulnerable functionality. Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-108099 requires a similar interaction with contributed modules or custom code and includes at least one known exploitation path that does not require authentication. Administrators are urged to update Drupal core to version 10.6.19, 11.3.19, or 11.4.10, depending on their release branch, and update Entity List to 3.0.10. "All versions of Drupal prior to 10.6.x, as well as all versions of Drupal 11 prior to 11.3.x, are end-of-life and no longer supported," the developer said The flaws also impact Drupal 12 pre-releases before beta2, but these are not meant to be used in production environments. The final stable 12.0 version will include fixes for both flaws. Administrators who cannot upgrade to a secure version are advised to uninstall Drupal’s core Field UI module (field_ui) as an effective mitigation measure. Also, Drupal Steward protects against some known attack vectors but does not cover every possible exploit. fxu3ve.text: Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a malicious npm package that's part of a recently disclosed software supply chain attack campaign dubbed MALFEX. The package, named "imgdecode," was uploaded to the package registry on September 30, 2026, by a user named "malfexteste8." It has been downloaded 979 times as of writing and is still available on npm as of writing. The latest version of the package is 1.0.3. "The npm package imgdecode hides a malicious loader in a compiled Node.js addon," SafeDep said. "Its nine-line JavaScript file loads a Windows dynamic-link library (DLL). When a Node.js program calls require('imgdecode') from a Windows console, the DLL attempts to download encrypted shellcode from GitHub. It decrypts the response and injects the result into a new dllhost.exe process." First documented by both Checkmarx and CloudSEK, MALFEX is the name assigned to a long-running campaign in which an unknown threat actor has been publishing malicious packages to npm since August 6, 2023, with an aim to compromise Windows systems. These packages were published across five npm publisher handles: malfexkkj, malfex_user, malfexteste2, malfexteste3, malfexteste4. Of the eight identified packages, three were found to act as a loader for Overlord RAT, while three others ("cdn-img-fetch," "img-to-native," and "native-runner") worked together to download and run a Node.js stealer. A third infection pathway involved the use of a postinstall hook to execute JavaScript capable of contacting an external server and retrieving an unspecified next-stage binary. Interestingly, the threat actor behind the campaign appears to be responding to public disclosures and npm removals by publishing replacements for "native-runner" and "img-to-native" within two days in the form of "runhelper" and "imgbundle." That same day, the first version of "imgdecode" was published. The timeline of events is as follows - September 26, 2026 - cdn-img-fetch, img-to-native, and native-runner 1.0.0 published September 28, 2026, at 4:06 p.m. UTC - npm removes native-runner and img-to-native September 30, 2026, at 3:29 a.m. UTC - imgbundle 1.0.0 published, replacing img-to-native September 30, 2026, at 3:37 a.m. UTC - runhelper 1.0.0 published, replacing native-runner September 30, 2026, at 4:13 p.m. UTC - runhelper unpublished September 30, 2026, at 10:32 p.m. UTC - imgdecode 1.0.0 published September 30, 2026, at 11:07 p.m. UTC - imgdecode 1.0.1 published October 1, 2026, at 5:48 p.m. UTC - imgdecode 1.0.2 published October 7, 2026, at 11:06 p.m. UTC - npm removes imgbundle October 8, 2026, at 1:03 p.m. UTC - npm removes cdn-img-fetch October 11, 2026, at 10:09 p.m. UTC - imgdecode 1.0.3 published The Node.js stealer chain is notable for the fact that none of the packages featured an install hook. Instead, the malicious code runs when "native-runner" is loaded. The package lists "img-to-native" as its dependency, which, in turn, has "img-to-native" as a dependency. The exact functionality of each of these packages is below - cdn-img-fetch downloads "banner.png" from a GitHub repository ("cavecrew/proj") and extracts an encrypted blob. img-to-native decrypts the blob using the key "malfexteam2027" and writes the contents to disk as a Go executable ("%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\node_runtime_helper.exe"). native-runner executes the Go executable, which then downloads the stealer binary ("setup.exe" aka movinlike) from "104.234.65[.]75:700." "Runhelper," advertised as a helper utility for "launching native binaries from Node.js projects," functions similarly to "native-runner" in that it's designed to run malicious code. Its primary responsibility is to locate a JPG file ("cdn-img-fetch/.runtime/rt.jpg"), extract shellcode from it, copy it into executable memory, and run it using Koffi, a Foreign Function Interface (FFI) module for Node.js. "Six hours after runhelper was unpublished, the operator published imgdecode with a compiled DLL to run the shellcode," SafeDep said. "From version 1.0.1, the DLL also downloads and decrypts the payload. Versions 1.0.1 and 1.0.2 still call require('imgbundle') before loading the DLL. Version 1.0.3 removes that dependency and needs no other MALFEX package." Like in the case of "runhelper," version 1.0.0 of "imgdecode" waits for "imgbundle" to write a file at the location "cdn-img-fetch/.runtime/" and, once it becomes available, reads its contents into memory, and passes them to a native Node.js addon for decoding the data. The addon is a 64-bit Microsoft Visual C++ (MSVC) DLL that first checks if it's running in a developer's terminal, and then proceeds to fetch a JPG file ("banner.jpg") from the same repository ("cavecrew/proj"), decrypt the embedded payload using the key "nif-runtime-2027," and ultimately inject the output into "dllhost.exe." "After decryption, the DLL checks the first bytes of the plaintext," SafeDep explained. "If they match a JPEG or PNG signature, the DLL stops. Inference: the operator could turn the loader off by serving encrypted content that decrypts to an image. Serving an ordinary image would instead generally cause decryption to fail before this check." Although the GitHub account "cavecrew" is no longer accessible, an Internet Archive screenshot of the image file dated October 6, 2026, shows that it's the same Go-based downloader used for retrieving the Node.js stealer and remote access tool ("movinlike") from "104.234.65[.]75:700." The Node.js application includes a .env file containing a command-and-control (C2) address ("104.234.65[.]75:7007") and a MALFEX license key, indicating the use of a malware builder or licensing system to craft such payloads. The malware runs anti-analysis checks that audit for the presence of virtual machines, sandboxes, and analysis tools like Process Monitor and Wireshark, before harvesting files matching seed phrases and specific extensions (.kdbx, .pem, .ppk, and .env), as well as data from Chromium-based web browsers, Discord, Telegram, cryptocurrency wallets, and gaming apps (Steam, Epic Games, Riot, Battle.net, Minecraft, and Ubisoft). It can also establish a WebSocket connection to the C2 server, allowing it to accept commands for shell execution, file transfer, process control, clipboard access, screenshots, and mouse and keyboard input. For persistence, it adds a Registry Run key and creates a scheduled task named "MicrosoftEdgeUpdateService." Developers who have installed any of the aforementioned packages should treat their Windows systems as potentially compromised, isolate them, check for persistence entries, rotate credentials, and transfer funds to new wallets if they seed phrases were stored in them,

kbwmt9.text: Cybersecurity researchers are sounding the alarm related to an active campaign in which unknown threat actors are abusing a compromised Microsoft 365 (M365) credential belonging to ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick) to gain unauthorized access to customers' M365 environments. ConnectWise Cloud Backup is a cloud-based backup and recovery service built for managed service providers (MSPs) to secure their clients' Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace data. To accomplish its tasks, the application is granted broad access to mailboxes, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, and directory data in every tenant on which it's installed. Huntress said it has observed confirmed unauthorized sign-ins within 173 partner/customer tenants using the compromised vendor credential. The incident impacts every organization that has the app installed, and the credential works against every tenant the app is consented in. "The app's credential is in hostile hands," security researcher Jonathan Semon said. "It was used to obtain Microsoft Graph tokens in customer tenants from 144.172.64[.]128 on October 15, between 06:13 and 08:34 UTC. The actor moved through tenants in sorted GUID order, a few seconds apart, which points to a script working from a target list." In the observed attackers, the adversary has been observed authenticating to the app using their own tooling, in a manner analogous to the backup service, and obtains tokens with the app's existing permissions. Given that the app has extensive permissions to access customer data, an attacker in possession of the tokens can read mailboxes, files, and directory data the backup service can. Huntress said the same IP address engaged in password spraying against four law firm tenants on October 13 and 14, 2026, although it said it detected no successful user sign-ins in its telemetry. In at least one partner tenant, the cybersecurity company said it found a separate ConnectWise app assigning itself Global Administrator privileges and adding credentials to other trusted applications within this environment, thereby opening a pathway to other privileged apps within customer environments. This effectively extends the risk beyond the vendor account. "The ConnectWise Cloud Management app for Microsoft Teams (application ID 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640) added itself to the Global Administrator role, then ran a Python script (User-Agent Python-urllib/3.12) that modified two other applications in the tenant: an MSP management application, and Huntress's own application (Huntress Security Platform), adding new client secrets to both," Semon explained. "The two applications that received new secrets are trusted, privileged tools. Adding a credential to an MSP management application can extend access beyond the one tenant, because those applications are often consented into the MSP's customers' tenants. A credential on a security tool's application gives the holder whatever that tool is permitted to do." Todyl, in a similar analysis, said it detected an unauthorized party authenticating to Microsoft Graph as the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application. "The access inherited the app's existing consent, which permits read/write access to mail and attachments (full mailbox access through Exchange Web Services), OneDrive and SharePoint files, and Teams chats, including the ability to restore data," Nicholas Koken, Todyl's head of Detection Engineering, said. "Revoking user sessions does not end this access. Disabling the app in a tenant stops new tokens from being issued there, though tokens already issued stay valid for up to 90 minutes. Any tenant where the app is still enabled stays exposed until ConnectWise rotates the credential." In response to the incident, ConnectWise has taken the step of closing Cloud Backup application access until further notice. The company said it has found no evidence that Cloud Backup partner backup data has been compromised. It has also shared the following steps to look for indicators of compromise - In the Microsoft Entra Admin Center, navigate to Monitoring → Sign-in logs, select the Service principal sign-ins tab, and filter by Application ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae. The default User sign-ins tab will not display the required information. In the IP address column, review authentication activity originating from IP addresses outside expected Microsoft/Azure ranges. The application's normal egress has been identified as Azure private IPv6. Suspicious IP address: 144.172.64[.]128 "The backup service needs broad access to do its job, and an attacker using its credentials will inherit that level of access for every tenant where the app is installed," Huntress explained. "Depending on the permissions in the tenant, that can include mailboxes, OneDrive and SharePoint files, Teams data, and directory information, much of it belonging to your clients. Some of that access, such as directory reads through Microsoft Graph, leaves no audit trail, which is why we suggest acting now instead of waiting for proof of access. The full potential impact depends on the permissions in play in each tenant." Users are recommended to disable the application until ConnectWise confirms all credentials have been reset, enable Microsoft Graph activity logs, audit for any new credentials added since October 13, 2026, and check Entra audit logs for ConnectWise or SkyKick applications adding themselves to a directory role. The development comes as Google's Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group, along with ManageEngine Threat Analysis Lab, detailed an "ephemeral supply chain tampering" of the update infrastructure belonging to AOMEI Backupper, a data backup, disk cloning, and disaster recovery software, to bypass traditional security defenses and deliver malware such as CROSSROAD and SHINYROAD. "The threat actor conducted repeated, short-burst configuration tampering against AOMEI origin servers," Google said. "Each tampering window remained active for only five to ten minutes before reverting to authentic versions. During the brief tampering windows, the threat actor modified the update settings file on the update server to redirect the software to download a malicious ZIP package from attacker-controlled servers instead of legitimate updates." The ZIP archive contains CROSSROAD, an initial downloader responsible for environment validation and staging follow-on payloads. It's also designed to establish scheduled task-based persistence to deploy SHINYROAD, a modular backdoor framework for covert command-and-control, via DLL sideloading. The software supply chain compromise campaign, which occurred between April and July 2026, has been attributed to a previously undocumented threat cluster codenamed UNC7017. The activity marks the first time that such a compromise has played out in brief intervals instead of maintaining a persistent, static modification on the servers. The campaign is assessed to have impacted organizations spanning a wide range of sectors, including IT services, telecommunications, higher education, and related entities in Australia, Brazil, India, Pakistan, Portugal, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, and the U.S. An Active Supply Chain Attack In a post on X, Microsoft said it's tracking an "active supply chain attack in which a threat actor compromised the trusted OAuth App of the backup application ConnectWise Cloud Backup (AppId: 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae), formerly SkyKick Backup, to obtain access tokens across customer tenants." The tech giant said the threat actor likely abused permissions previously granted by customers to the application, including highly privileged permissions like Directory.ReadWrite.All. "On October 15, 2026, we observed broad successful service principal authentication originating from the IP address 144.172.64[.]128," it added. "Follow-on activity included Microsoft Graph API reconnaissance and attempts to add additional credentials on the related service principal in target tenants to maintain direct access as a backdoor." Microsoft is recommending that security teams review service principal sign-ins from unrecognized IP addresses, app credential changes, and OAuth grant activity associated with the aforementioned OAuth AppId. ConnectWise, in a separate advisory, confirmed it has identified unauthorized access to application identities within the ConnectWise Cloud Backup environment. It has shut off Cloud Backup application access while its "investigation and remediation efforts remain ongoing." (This is a developing story. Please check back for more details.)

u1g9gw.text: Researchers warn that hackers could soon exploit a maximum-severity vulnerability (CVE-2026-103849) affecting Magento and Adobe Commerce, potentially allowing them to execute arbitrary PHP code on store servers. According to e-commerce security firm Sansec, attacks leveraging the vulnerability, dubbed BlockStrap, have not yet been observed, but threat actors are expected to find a way to exploit it. The researchers based their assessment on identifying four potential attack paths involving CVE-2026-103849 in less than 24 hours. The flaw impacts September versions of Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source through 2.4.9 and Adobe Commerce B2B through 1.5.3. The security firm warned that Adobe’s “priority 2” rating of this flaw does not reflect the danger and urgency in this case, despite the more complex attack path. “The attack path is complex, but anyone with an AI agent can reverse-engineer the patch into working exploits in a relatively short time,” stated Sansec states. “That is why we question Adobe's priority 2 rating (patch within 30 days). StyleSmuggler went from a priority 1 hotfix to mass exploitation in three days, and BlockStrap is of similar complexity.” Adobe’s bulletin, published on October 13, describes the flaw as an improper neutralization of special elements used in a template engine, leading to arbitrary code execution. Sansec explains that BlockStrap is a second-pass template engine directive injection that allows attacker-controlled content in a child email template to be signed and processed again at the root level, executing a smuggled {{block}} directive. According to Sansec’s analysis, BlockStrap exposes a gap left by the StyleSmuggler fix in the same email-template engine. Adobe’s fix replaces the generic processing with registered placeholders, preventing exploitation. Sansec says that a plain Composer install isn’t enough to address the risk, and website administrators must apply the 2026-oct release or Adobe’s isolated patch. “BlockStrap and StyleSmuggler are separate fixes. You need both, so keep the September VULN-39341 hotfix in place as well,” Sansec cautions. The e-commerce security company says it will provide an update when it detects mass attack waves, which it expects to occur soon. 39bjr.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 16, 2026Vulnerability / OpenBSD A local privilege escalation exploit published today gains root on OpenBSD 7.9 by chaining a roughly 37-year-old integer overflow with a separate kernel flaw, bypassing OpenBSD's KARL kernel-address randomization and its SMAP and SMEP hardware protections. Security firm Calif, which found and reported the flaws, published a detailed writeup and full proof-of-concept code after OpenBSD shipped patches for both issues in September. The integer overflow in the shmat(4) attach function was fixed in errata 018, shipped September 14 as a reliability fix. The reference-counting use-after-free that completes the chain was fixed separately in errata 026, shipped September 30 as a security fix. Both are available through syspatch and cover all architectures. OpenBSD 7.8 also received the integer-overflow fix. The integer overflow, the entry point for the full chain, is classified as a reliability fix, not a security fix. No CVE has been assigned for either flaw as of publication. There is no evidence that the vulnerabilities have been used in attacks. The shared-memory attachment counter shm_nattch is defined as a signed 16-bit short with a maximum value of 32,767 in original BSD sources dating to 1988. OpenBSD inherited the type and never widened it. The exploit maps 127 shared-memory segments and forks 259 processes, pushing the counter past its maximum and wrapping it to −32,643. A race condition then triggers a use-after-free: the corrupted reference count causes the kernel to free memory that other processes still use. A separate out-of-bounds write overwrites multicast-membership counters in the kernel. When the affected socket closes, the resulting decrements modify page-table entries, switching a user-memory mapping to supervisor-accessible and bypassing SMAP and SMEP. The exploit then overwrites a function pointer at a predictable kernel address to run its own code. "While OpenBSD's KARL relinks the kernel binary to randomize both function and data addresses, the kernel's memory allocators remain deterministic," researcher Andrew Griffiths wrote. Both the boot-time and best-fit allocators lack base-address randomization, so early-boot structures, including function pointers in the lo0 and enc0 network-interface handlers, land at the same addresses across reboots on the same hardware. The exploit needs no information-disclosure vulnerability. Beyond the two errata, Calif proposes four categories of hardening: safe-unlinking for kernel linked lists (already used by FreeBSD and NetBSD), randomization of the page-table self-referential mapping, kernel-allocator randomization, and compiler-based bounds checking. Calif said it reported the flaws to OpenBSD "earlier this year." The proof-of-concept exploit code is available on GitHub.

hael9w.text: Candiru spyware was delivered to devices at Al Jazeera Media Network via targeted online advertisements in a zero-click attack that required only rendering the malicious ads on the victim's device. Researchers at Citizen Labs investigating the attacks referred to this technique as AdFection, noting that their report is the first public technical confirmation of mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. A similar method was documented in late 2025 by Amnesty International, involving ads that infected targets with Predator spyware without them clicking anything. That infection mechanism was called Aladdin and surfaced due to a collection of marketing files and documents leaked from the Intellexa surveillance company that researchers studied and corroborated with technical details from forensic investigations. Unlike Alladin, AdFection was caught in real attacks and linked to Israeli firm Discovere-Tech, described by Citizen Lab as " a bridge between mercenary spyware companies and the advertising ecosystem." Ads participating in AdFectionSource: Citizen Lab Zero-click Candiru spyware infection According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech allowed its customers to use its Controlium platform to target specific devices with malicious code, or profile, deanonimize, and fingerprint user devices. "Discover-Tech appears to work with multiple mercenary spyware, hacking, and advertising vendors, connecting the spyware industry to the online advertising ecosystem," Citizen Lab says. The company purchased ad placements through mainstream ad networks and exchanges, embedding JavaScript in ads that contacted its "NOAS server" when rendered. Using multiple parameters (e.g., IP address, ad identifiers), the NOAS server, "or getAd server," determined if a target was eligible to receive JavaScript code. Selected targets received additional code, while other devices the ad rendered on received nothing, helping keep the attacks stealthy. Action sequence for valid targetsSource: Citizen Lab Al Jazeera provided Citizen Lab with evidence of attacks that targeted at least 45 devices between 2024 and 2025. The network logs examined by the researchers showed a sequence from Discover-Tech infrastructure to Candiru validation servers and then to spyware command-and-control servers. The researchers also recovered a DLL file from a compromised Windows system and attributed it with high confidence to Candiru, based on infrastructure and code overlaps with previously captured samples. Candiru is an Israeli spyware vendor that sells surveillance tools, officially only to governments. The company also developed malware for Windows called DevilsTongue, which can steal files, credentials, and messages. According to past reports, its tools have been deployed through Windows and Chrome zero-day exploits against journalists, activists, politicians, and other targets. Candiru attack chainSource: Citizen Lab While Al Jazeera is one confirmed target of these attacks, Citizen Lab reports that the advertising operation placed 3.77 billion bids and won 442 million auctions between March and June 2026. Ads assessed to carry attacker script tags appeared across 75,373 Android/iOS apps and 120,768 websites, although these figures do not represent infection counts. “We estimate that between hundreds of thousands and millions of users were directed to these domains via Discover-Tech ads,” explains Citizen Lab. After receiving Citizen Lab's reports, major advertising companies like Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, Eskimi, and Vungle took action to remove offending accounts and block access to domains. oyxhl2.text: Attackers repeatedly changed the files that AOMEI Backupper fetches from the vendor's own update servers, in windows of five to ten minutes at a time between May and July 2026, so that any copy of the Windows backup program that checked for an update during one of those windows would download and run a backdoor. Google Threat Intelligence Group, Mandiant, and ManageEngine's Threat Analysis Lab, which disclosed the campaign this week, say AOMEI has reported fixing its servers, but that fix does not remove the backdoor from machines that were already hit. AOMEI Backupper is Windows backup and disk-cloning software made by AOMEI Technology, a vendor registered in Hong Kong. Like the company's remote-desktop tool AnyViewer, it runs background services that regularly check AOMEI's servers over HTTPS for software updates and promotional pop-ups. Two files drive that check. One, down_html.ini, names the update package to download and the checksum the program uses to verify it. The other, Notifycfg.ini, tells the pop-up service what to display and what to run. The program does not cryptographically verify either file, and the checksum that is supposed to prove the download is genuine sits inside the same unsigned file that names it. Nothing in the software was exploited. There was no vulnerability, and no user action was needed beyond having the program installed and running, according to ManageEngine's lab.
