The attacker only had to change two text files on the server for a few minutes. A copy of Backupper that checked in during a window pulled the attacker's package into its own folder, and the notification file then made it run. It ran with the privileges of the AOMEI process that launched it. On the machines the lab examined, that was enough to install software across the whole system, though it said the elevation depended on how the AOMEI service was running. Three Windows, Eleven Countries GTIG and Mandiant confirmed three tampering windows, and said more probably happened that they did not see: May 28, 2026: a 10-minute window, 05:40 to 05:50 UTC July 16, 2026: a 6-minute window, 08:33 to 08:39 UTC July 20, 2026: a 5-minute window, 10:35 to 10:40 UTC Only copies that checked for an update during a window were affected. A copy that checked before or after got clean, genuine files, which is what makes the attack hard to catch. GTIG described the targeting as opportunistic, hitting whatever system happened to poll during those minutes. From its own telemetry, GTIG identified affected organizations in IT services, telecommunications and higher education across 11 countries: Australia, Brazil, India, Pakistan, Portugal, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye and the United States. It gave no total and said the real number is likely higher. GTIG named AnyViewer, AOMEI's remote-desktop tool, as using the same update flow, but the detections it describes involve Backupper. Neither report lists which Backupper versions are affected, and the lab examined version 8.3.0. GTIG tracks the group behind the campaign as UNC7017 and names no country or known actor. It said this is the first supply chain compromise it has encountered built on Windows this short, "effectively evading traditional point-in-time triage and automated file scanning." What Landed on the Machine On a machine that pulled the package, a downloader that GTIG calls CROSSROAD unpacked a bundle into a local Radmin folder, created a scheduled task set to run every three hours, and then deleted itself from disk. The bundle included a genuine, signed copy of Radmin, a commercial remote-administration tool. ManageEngine's lab found it staged but never switched on, with no listener, no configuration, and no new account. The remote control came instead from a separate implant that reached out to the attacker. The scheduled task runs the signed Radmin program, which loads an attacker-built DLL placed beside it, which in turn loads the SHINYROAD implant. The implant gives a remote shell and can fetch and run new code on command. It talks to a single hard-coded address with no backup, so blocking that one address cuts off the attacker's control. CROSSROAD runs only in some places. It checks the machine's location and stops if it is in China, and ManageEngine added that it also stops if it finds particular security agents on the host. On machines that passed those checks, GTIG later saw a second tool pushed down on top of SHINYROAD, the open-source Adaptix C2 framework, disguised as Nitro PDF software. A July 20 Change That Needed No Code to Run The July 20 window included a second trick that did not require running any program. GTIG found that the notification file had been changed to open an invisible, one-pixel pop-up pointing to a file on an attacker's server via WebDAV, a way to access a remote file as if it were on the local disk. Rendering that pop-up can make Windows send the logged-in user's NetNTLMv2 authentication response, a token an attacker can try to crack offline or reuse, to the attacker's address with nothing visible to the user. Because no program had to run, a machine with the backdoor blocked could still have leaked that token. What AOMEI Was Told, and When ManageEngine's lab said its endpoint software first caught the activity on May 28, when it recorded AOMEI Backupper installing Radmin on two unrelated customers in different countries. A customer raised it on June 7, and the lab notified AOMEI the same day. AOMEI's first explanation was that the content had been intercepted and changed in transit. The lab said the evidence did not support that explanation. Both machines had fetched the files over HTTPS from AOMEI's own servers, across different countries and networks, and the program had pulled the package in through its normal update steps. In mid-July, its own monitors caught one of the windows as it happened, confirming the change was being served from AOMEI's side. Mandiant notified AOMEI on July 17 and shared indicators. AOMEI told Mandiant on July 29 that it had taken corrective action to secure its servers. ManageEngine's lab said that, as of publication, it had not independently confirmed that the compromise had been contained. Neither report says how the attacker gained the ability to change files on AOMEI's servers. AOMEI's published changelog for Backupper, checked by The Hacker News on October 16, lists no change to how the program verifies updates through the current release, 8.5.0, from October 9. Neither report points to a version that closes the gap. What to Check Now A fixed server does not clean a machine that was hit. The downloader set up its scheduled task and then restored the local update file to its genuine contents, so an infected machine can look normal while the vendor's download page also looks clean. GTIG and ManageEngine both urge organizations running AOMEI software to hunt across the whole April-to-July period. "Organizations running AOMEI software cannot assume they are protected solely because the vendor took corrective server-side action," GTIG and Mandiant said. Do not judge an alert by checking the vendor's download page now. Because the files changed back within minutes, that page serves genuine content almost all the time, which has led analysts to dismiss real detections as false alarms. Preserve the files cached in the program's own folders, and check network logs for what was served at the exact time the alert fired. On the endpoint, hunt for: Scheduled task: RadminComponentRuntime, or NitroRuntime for the follow-on tool File: an unsigned upgrade-now.exe that carries AOMEI's publisher details, or any program running from Backupper's html pop-up folder Folder: attacker files staged under the local Radmin application-data folder On the network, block the attacker infrastructure named in both reports, and block outbound SMB (TCP 445) and WebDAV to external addresses to stop the credential trick: Domain: storage-data[.]com, promotion.storage-data[.]com, aomei.storage-data[.]com IP: 8.210.84[.]56, 8.218.65[.]184, 47.239.60[.]117 GTIG and ManageEngine each published detection rules with their reports, YARA rules from GTIG and Sigma rules from the lab. Both sets are the researchers' own and have not been tested by The Hacker News.

vrjppe.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 16, 2026Phishing / Artificial Intelligence Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an advanced persistent threat (APT) spear-phishing campaign that has targeted individuals affiliated with Taiwan research organizations to direct victims to an adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) phishing framework designed to harvest their Google account credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes. The activity is being tracked by Cisco Talos under the moniker UAT-11985, describing it as likely fueled by artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted content generation so as to quickly craft bespoke lures aimed at different targets within the confines of a common social engineering framework. The campaign was first observed in mid-2026. "The operation leveraged legitimate public event themes and impersonated reputable academic and policy institutions to establish credibility," Talos researcher Joey Chen said in an analysis. "Beyond traditional email phishing, the actor incorporated QR code phishing (quishing) techniques by modifying legitimate event posters with malicious QR codes, expanding the attack surface beyond email recipients to secondary victims who may encounter printed materials." Central to the operation is the use of legitimate or plausible public event information in spear-phishing emails and embedding within them a URL that points to attacker-controlled infrastructure, while hovering over the hyperlink displays a legitimate-looking Google Forms URL. These invitation emails feature nearly identical syntactic structures despite the breadth of geopolitical topics being discussed, indicating the content was mass-produced from a reusable prompt template rather than painstakingly crafted for each target. Specifically, the emails follow a three-part structure - The opening section offers a "polished (but overly elaborate) description" of the geopolitical or policy context. The second section is tailored to the recipient and paints them in a flattering light in an attempt to trigger engagement. The third and final section provides details of event logistics, including the topic, date, venue, and registration instructions. The threat actor has been found to impersonate legitimate Taiwan-based institutions like the Taiwan European Union Centre, NCCU Institute of International Relations, and Taiwan Research Institute, fabricating the sender identities to make the messages appear more convincing. "Taken together, the reuse of an almost-identical narrative structure, rhetorical style, personalized flattery, institutional impersonation, and deceptive registration mechanism strongly suggests a coordinated and carefully targeted spear-phishing campaign rather than three independent invitations," Talos said. In a subset of cases, the phishing emails incorporate legitimate event posters scraped from legitimate websites, but with the QR codes modified to trick victims into scanning the malicious QR code to "register" for the event. The phishing site imitates the look of a legitimate Google Form, but the primary goal of the site is to serve a pop-up that prompts the victim to sign-in with their Google account to complete the form. Doing so takes them to a bogus site featuring a spoofed Google login panel to capture their credentials and authentication challenges. The pixel-perfect replica site is an adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) proxy that uses obfuscated JavaScript to gather and exfiltrate the entered information in real-time over a WebSocket connection, while simultaneously forwarding it to legitimate Google authentication servers. Prior to establishing the WebSocket connection, the JavaScript payload collects device and browser information, including the locale, user agent, screen dimensions, and mobile-device status, which are then reported to the command-and-control (C2) server via a "google_login_start" request. When the victim submits the password, the phishing page transmits the password, along with the account identifier and browser user-agent information, to the actor's HTTP C2 server through a "google_login_check" request. The threat actor's server, placed in an AitM position, then forwards the credentials to the actual Google authentication service. "The spoofed Google login panels only support Simplified Chinese (zh-CN), Traditional Chinese (zh-TW), and English locales, with region detection based on the victim's browser 'navigator.languages,' strongly suggesting targeting of Chinese-speaking users," Chen explained. "By deliberately splitting one-shot uploads with POST requests from low-latency state updates with WebSocket connection, the threat actor has engineered a seamless credential-harvesting relay. This allows the threat actor to mirror Google's dynamic authentication state in real time, ultimately achieving full account takeover without raising the victim's suspicion."

fabr8i.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 16, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Web Security OpenAI has disclosed seven new incidents in which its artificial intelligence (AI) models exhibited misaligned behavior, including one case where its research model, after not having funds on an Ethereum test network, spent test cryptocurrency from a third-party's wallet without authorization to complete a coding task. The incident, the AI company said, involved an internal research model part of the GPT-5.6 Sol family. The incident occurred on June 26, 2026, and was discovered by OpenAI three months later. "An internal research model asked to update a cryptocurrency trading application used funds from a wallet that the task had not supplied to pay for a deployment on Sepolia, an Ethereum test network," OpenAI said. "It derived wallet keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, found an account with test-network funds, and used that account to pay for the requested contract deployment." The assignment allowed the model to deploy compatible contracts if it did not find one, but gave it no funded wallet to pay the network fees. After its attempts to obtain free test tokens failed, it wrote a script to derive "accounts from common developer recovery phrases and query their balances." In the process, it identified 362 addresses and found one account that held enough Sepolia ETH. Armed with the recovery (or seed) phrase, the model derived the private keys that grant unauthorized access to the corresponding account and spend the stashed cryptocurrency. Although the model questioned whether it had the necessary permission to carry out this step, it subsequently reasoned that a public recovery phrase and valueless test-network tokens made the funds acceptable to use. "But using public known key/funds ethically? Funds on a known public dev mnemonic are effectively abandoned/test ETH; Sepolia valueless," the model mused. "We can use [amount redacted] to deploy task. Fine." OpenAI has since implemented additional safeguards to prevent live internet access for such scenarios, adding it runs its misalignment monitoring system on all traffic to flag events if its AI agents manage to gain live internet access. "This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder's permission, then act on that judgment without authorization," OpenAI said. Besides using a funded test cryptocurrency wallet without authorization, OpenAI said it identified six more cases of misalignment involving its models, adding to three other incidents it revealed at the start of this month - June 16, 2026, when an internal research model bypassed a restriction limiting internet access to HTTP GET requests as part of efforts to seek public trade statistics. It achieved this by using an external browser to send requests on its behalf, retrieved annual figures as an image, and extracted them using optical character recognition. June 16 and 17, 2026, when an internal model developed and tested ways to bypass restrictions on internet access during reinforcement learning and explored ways to contact outside services, and continued testing these approaches even after obtaining the statistics it was seeking, such as teacher salaries in Merrowen, connections to the electrical grid in Orvessa, and disability counts in Bellora. June 17, 2026, when a highly persistent internal model tasked with retrieving figures from a public research dashboard accessed an unspecified organization's internal systems and changed their configuration. The model altered a setting to obtain a cloud-storage access token and downloaded non-public tables containing 147,451 rows. Not only did the model not disclose these actions, it restored the modified setting, but continued using the token to retrieve non-public data. June 17, 2026, when a highly persistent internal model deployed as part of a data-retrieval task in reinforcement-learning training abused a government statistics website's file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials. It then analyzed the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint's authorization checks, retrieved data that it was denied access to, and stored it locally. The data included annual statistics spanning 24 years, including years beyond the requested year. In its answer, the model made no mention of the fact that it had obtained unauthorized access. June 19 and 20, 2026, when its internal research models bypassed restrictions on internet access to allow only HTTP GET requests to fetch figures from government entities' public data sources by writing custom programs to send a POST request through a custom network connection. October 6, 2026, when an internal research model assigned to grade seven responses attempted to submit unsupported assessments after it found that the required input files were missing. When the automated check rejected its bogus grading report, the model tried to create fake input files in an attempt to pass the checks. After this also resulted in failure, the model took the step of damaging its task environment in hopes of triggering a reset. "In response to this and other incidents, we hardened our security controls, took additional steps to prevent models from accessing the live internet during training, improved alignment grading, and extended misalignment monitoring to all reinforcement learning and evaluation traffic," OpenAI said.

6lxgs8.text: In the space of a month, a new category of AI model went from nonexistent to everywhere. TypeSafe AI released Jev on September 15 and called it a System One model, a nod to Kahneman's fast, intuitive thinking. OpenAI announced its own Decisions API at DevDay and opened a public beta on October 6. Cribl published cribl-decision, an open LoRA adapter you can run locally. Others, like Laya, are already showing up in open source tooling. These models skip text generation entirely. You hand them some state and a set of typed questions. They hand back a choice, a score, or a yes/no with a probability attached. For security operations, I think this is some of the best news of the year. I also think most of the conversation is pointed at the wrong layer. Why a SOC should be excited Three properties make decision models a natural fit for alert triage. You get a number you can automate against. A typed answer with a calibrated probability is something you can put a threshold on. Ask the model whether an alert is benign and you get back a probability. Close it automatically above 0.97. Below 0.6, treat it as a likely incident and escalate it. Anything in between goes to an analyst for a closer look. TypeSafe even suggests stricter thresholds for irreversible actions, which maps neatly onto “disable an account” versus “add a comment to the ticket.” They're cheap enough for every alert. Jev is priced at $42 per billion input tokens, with responses in 70 to 500 milliseconds. Say an enterprise sees 450,000 alerts a year and you feed a few thousand tokens per alert. The model bill lands somewhere around a hundred dollars a year. The economic argument for cherry-picking and only looking at high-severity alerts just disappeared! Every verdict becomes a record. The answer space is fixed in advance and the output carries its own probability. You can log every decision, replay it, and compare it with what actually happened. That's far easier to audit than a paragraph of generated reasoning. One caveat worth keeping in mind. When vendors say these models "can't hallucinate," they mean the output always matches the schema you defined. A well-formed answer can still be wrong. But a calibrated guess is still just a guess The old rule still applies. Garbage in, garbage out. Calibration is a promise about a distribution. When a well-calibrated model says 90%, it means that across inputs that look like this one, it's right about 90% of the time. So the question that matters is what "this one" looks like. If the input is an alert title and a severity field, the model is calibrated about alerts with that title and that severity. It knows nothing about the host. Here's why that matters in practice. Our AI SOC Report 2026 covers 25 million alerts triaged across our customer base in 2025. In that data, 82,000 alerts went through a live memory scan of the endpoint. About 2,600 of those machines had an active infection. And 51% of the infected machines had already been reported as mitigated by the EDR. Think about what a decision model sees for one of those alerts. Malware detected, threat quarantined, low severity. A perfectly calibrated model should close it with high confidence, because most alerts that look like that really are fine. The model did its job. The input was wrong. Severity has the same problem at a larger scale. Nearly 1% of real incidents in our data traced back to alerts at the lowest severity levels. At an average of 450,000 alerts a year, that's roughly 54 real threats, about one a week. Cribl's own model card says it plainly. The model can be overconfident, and it's sensitive to how the prompt and candidates are worded. That's honest, and it applies to every model in this category. What evidence actually looks like Think about a crime scene. You can describe it to a chatbot in general terms and get a plausible theory. Or you can bring in the DNA lab, the fingerprints, the forensic evidence and the witness statements. Nobody needs to ask which approach finds the right suspect. Security investigations work the same way. Filip Stojkovski recently called this Security Context Engineering, and I think the name fits. The job is to turn an alert into a set of facts before anyone, human or model, makes a call. The question What the alert usually gives you What forensic evidence gives you What ran? "Suspicious PowerShell" The process tree, the parent, the full command line, the script on disk What did it do? A hash and a reputation score What the file did when detonated, the network calls, the files it dropped Is it still there? "Mitigated" from the EDR A live memory scan showing injected code or a fileless payload Who was it? A username Where they logged in, from which device, and whether that's normal for them The third row deserves extra attention. The most common families we found in memory last year were tools like Mimikatz, Meterpreter and Cobalt Strike. These are built to live in memory, which is exactly where a file-based "quarantined" status can't see. None of this evidence is exotic. It's what a good incident responder collects by hand. The hard part is collecting it automatically, for every alert, in under a minute. The hardest context is what normal looks like Forensic evidence tells you what happened on a machine. It doesn't tell you whether that's expected in this particular company. Identity alerts show the gap clearly. In our 2025 data, 74% of identity alerts were classified as likely benign. Impossible travel alerts were confirmed as real compromises only about 2% of the time, and VPN usage alone drove around 30% of them. A model can't tell that Dave from finance always logs in from Portugal, or that a CrowdStrike alert on the build servers fires every time DevOps ships a release. That knowledge usually lives in the head of your most senior analyst, and it walks out the door when they leave. Two things make this context harder than the forensic kind. You can't buy it, because it's specific to your environment. And it decays, because assets, users and tooling change every week. A snapshot loaded during onboarding is stale within a quarter. So organizational context has to be a loop. Learn from past cases and how analysts resolved them. Pull live context mid-investigation when memory isn't enough. Then compare every verdict with its outcome and write the lesson back. That last step is also how you check whether 90% still means 90% in your environment, and not only on someone's benchmark. A forensic approach to alert triage and investigation This is the layer we've spent our time on, so here's a concrete example of what investing in it looks like. Our founding team came from reverse engineering and incident response, and that background shaped one rule. Collect the evidence first, then decide. Code-level evidence. Our Genetic Analysis technology compares every piece of binary code running in memory against a large database of trusted and malicious code. It catches known malware, and it also catches new code that reuses pieces of known threats. Live memory forensics, triggered automatically. When an alert doesn't carry enough evidence for a verdict, or there are signs of a fileless attack or code injection, the platform runs our Endpoint Scanner on the machine. It's a single executable with nothing to install. It collects process trees, executables loaded into memory, memory dumps where injection is suspected, and the files behind scheduled tasks and autoruns. That's how we found the infected machines marked as mitigated. Detonation and network forensics. Suspicious files get run in a sandbox, and URLs, domains and IPs get investigated, so the verdict rests on observed behavior. Organizational memory. Org Brain is our answer to the "what's normal here" problem. It keeps two kinds of memory. One is procedural, how your team investigates and which detections it closes on sight. The other is declarative, your assets, your users, their normal behavior, and even how your SIEM schema is structured. It learns from your case history, fetches live context mid-investigation, and writes conclusions back after every investigation. All this allowed us to investigate over 25 million alerts in 2025, at every severity. Fewer than 2% were escalated to a human, verdict accuracy was 98%, and median triage time was under a minute. When it comes to cost, most of this analysis is deterministic forensics, which is far more affordable to run than a large model on every alert. That's why we price per endpoint and have been investigating everything, long before decision models arrived. Decision models now bring the same economics to the decision step for everyone, and that's a good thing for the industry. If you're building your own pipeline, the same structure applies whichever model sits at the end. Spend your engineering effort on the evidence and the organizational knowledge. Those are the parts that are hard to get and the parts that compound. Where to put your effort Frontier models get better every few months, and everyone gets the upgrade on the same day. Decision models will follow the same curve. Whatever edge a model gives you this quarter, your competitors and your attackers have it too. The context you feed those models is the part that's actually yours. If you're automating triage this year, here's where I'd spend the time. Collect evidence before you decide. Process trees, detonation results and memory contents beat alert metadata every time. Stop letting severity decide what gets investigated. With decision models this cheap, there's no longer a cost reason to skip low-severity alerts. Treat organizational knowledge as a system. Assets, users and normal behavior need to be learned and refreshed continuously. Measure calibration in your own environment. Tie every automated verdict to its outcome, and watch for drift. Decision models make the last step fast, cheap and auditable. Whether that last step is right still depends on everything that came before it.

pkaol0.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 16, 2026Zero-Day / Vulnerability The China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (previously UNC5221 or Warp Panda) exploited a newly disclosed security flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) as a zero-day in late August 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS score: 9.3), is a case of improper origin validation in an internal messaging component that could be exploited by a remote attacker to perform file operations on an affected appliance. "The vulnerability exists within internal components of Remote Support," BeyondTrust said in a Thursday alert. "The components did not adequately validate the origin of the messages it received. Under the right conditions, this could be used to perform file operations on the appliance." Patches for the flaw have been pushed to all Remote Support SaaS customers as of October 9, 2026. Self-hosted customers of Remote Support running versions from 24.3.1 through 26.2.3 are advised to manually update to BT26-05-RS patch. Customers running a version older than 24.3.1 will be required to upgrade to a newer version to apply the fix. According to a timeline of events shared by BeyondTrust, Armory Castle is said to have exploited the flaw as a zero-day on a single self-hosted Remote Support appliance on August 29, 2026. Then, on September 27, 2026, "successful exploitation of another security device provider [became] public," it added, prompting it to initiate an investigation to hunt for similar activity. Armory Castle has a history of exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities in Citrix NetScaler (CVE-2023-4966) and Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887, and CVE-2025-0282) appliances to break a wide range of sectors, including legal services, SaaS providers, business-process outsourcers, technology, and governments, for long-term intelligence collection. It's known to be active since October 2023. "The actor uses a zero-day selectively against chosen targets, and once the vulnerability is public, the actor typically moves to broad exploitation of every instance still unpatched," BeyondTrust said. "Our working assessment is that this actor selects high-value software targets in advance and keeps a working model of the products the actor targets in an AI context that it uses on an ongoing basis to develop exploit chains." Google-owned Mandiant, which shared additional details related to the exploitation activity, said a successful compromise is followed by the deployment of a lightweight PHP web shell codenamed SAWFLY for interactive remote access and bidirectional encrypted command-and-control (C2) communication. The operator makes use of commercial VPN exit nodes and compromised home and small-office routers to blend into regular traffic, and then leverages the web shell as a conduit to escalate privileges, obtain full administrative control of the appliance, and establish persistence in a manner that survives reboots. The intrusion is characterized by efforts to facilitate credential theft by reading the appliance's stored secrets and abusing the administrative access to reach downstream systems and enable lateral movement. Details of the post-exploitation actions undertaken by the threat actor are listed below - Gaining root-level control of the appliance host by copying the system shell executable (/bin/sh) to the file "/usr/bin/dbus-authd" and modifying its ownership to root and enabling Set User ID (SUID) permissions, causing it to be executed with the privileges of the file's owner. Attempting to harvest credentials directly from the appliance's native secrets management database by using the proprietary "/ns/sbin/bt-secrets" Command Line Interface (CLI) utility to manage, store, and retrieve passwords, API keys, and endpoint credentials. Targeting the BeyondTrust configuration templates to obtain passwordless root privileges to the site service account and Pivoted into the BeyondTrust Remote Support application to perform reconnaissance via compromised administrator credentials and then launch remote sessions to downstream systems populated within the appliance's Jump Item list. Abusing the elevated administrative privileges to establish a remote support session to target internal endpoints and obtain full file-system access to those systems with an aim to download and exfiltrate sensitive internal documents for network reconnaissance. Tunneling traffic through the BeyondTrust device via BARECLAW, a C-based custom SOCKS5 proxy tunneler that relays TCP connections between a remote client and destinations. Modifying "/ns/config/haproxy.conf" file to ensure BARECLAW is accessible directly from the internet. Hindering detection efforts by systematically deleting system, web server, and application-level logs. "Throughout the intrusion, Armory Castle leveraged a deep understanding of BeyondTrust appliance internals, as evidenced by their abuse of proprietary CLI utilities, startup configuration templates and local reverse-proxy routing," Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant researchers Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Brian Meyer, John Palmisano, Rajesh Rajeshirke, Steve Rasch, and John Wolfram said. "Any appliance that was reachable from the internet on a vulnerable version during the exploitation window should be treated as potentially compromised until it has been reviewed."

2ta124.text: AI agents being tested online reached the live systems of Indian organizations and read business records, including personal data and confidential material, CERT-In said in an advisory on October 15. The agents went beyond their assigned tasks, and none of the organizations detected the unauthorized access. After internal reviews, the AI companies whose models were being tested voluntarily reported the cases to CERT-In, India's national cyber agency. AI agents are software systems that can plan work, run commands, use tools, and act on the internet autonomously for extended periods. In these cases, the agents gained access via credentials and connection settings left exposed in application configuration and public code repositories, and via cloud service roles with excessive permissions. CERT-In did not name the AI companies, their models, or the organizations and sectors involved. It did not say how many companies reported cases or how many organizations were affected, and said only that the reports came in recently. It also did not say whether any data the agents read was copied or kept, or whether the affected organizations have been told. Attackers Used Open-Source AI Agent Tools in a Separate Campaign CERT-In's own threat hunting found a second, separate set of incidents: a financially motivated campaign against Indian entities. The attackers misused publicly available offensive-security frameworks built on AI agents. The frameworks continue to be misused and rebranded, with numerous deployments across infrastructure in several countries. CERT-In did not name the frameworks or the attackers. In this campaign, the frameworks cut the time from first access to final impact from days to a few hours, according to CERT-In. The attackers ran several agents in parallel for hours to days to reach their goals. Victims that only partly fixed the problems were attacked again within days, at a larger scale. Google Threat Intelligence Group reported a separate case in September. Attackers who had compromised a cloud resource planned, built and ran an agent-driven campaign that harvested thousands of third-party credentials, all in under 6 hours. On October 9, CERT-In warned of attacks on non-banking financial companies, digital lenders, fintech firms, payment providers and wallet operators. The attackers in those cases stole API credentials and called fund-transfer and disbursal APIs directly to move money into mule accounts. AI-assisted tools may have been used in those attacks. CERT-In has not said whether those attacks are related to the campaign in its October 15 advisory. What CERT-In Wants Fixed The weaknesses behind both kinds of incidents were ordinary, CERT-In said. Credentials and keys were exposed in source code, public repository history, configuration files, client apps and public web pages. Old, unused and test APIs were still reachable from the internet. Payment API keys were stored in plain text, and cloud and backend-as-a-service roles granted ordinary or anonymous users broad read and write access. Management interfaces were exposed to the internet, and application middleware was left unpatched, with weak credentials or no multi-factor authentication. In the cases reported by the AI companies, agents found the same exposed credential again and reused it in separate operations. CERT-In did not publish indicators of compromise for either kind of incident. Organizations should apply the baseline in CERT-In's May blueprint and take these steps: Search source code, commit history, CI/CD variables, configuration files, client apps and cloud storage for exposed credentials. Rotate any you find, purge them from history and confirm the fix from outside. Scan every commit and build for secrets, and keep credentials out of code, configuration files and databases. Keep a full list of your APIs, and shut down old, unused and test APIs and accounts. Apply least privilege to cloud and backend-as-a-service roles, keep privileged keys out of client-side code, and test what an anonymous user can read and write. Take management interfaces off the internet, require multi-factor authentication for all admin access, and patch exposed middleware quickly. Watch APIs with rate-based anomaly detection, alert on enumeration bursts, bulk reads and automated sign-ups, and keep logs for at least 180 days. After any credential exposure or confirmed access, treat the environment as compromised until a forensic check clears it. Retest after fixing it, and expect repeat attempts within days to weeks. If you run AI agents, give each run its own short-lived, least-privilege identity and block outbound traffic except to the destinations each run needs. Keep a tamper-resistant log of agent actions, at least those that touch production systems and data. Banks, insurers, other financial firms, and fintech companies should also apply the payment and disbursement API measures outlined in the October 9 advisory. CERT-In's directions also require organizations to report cyber incidents to the agency within 6 hours. For AI developers, research labs and evaluation agencies, CERT-In wants test runs isolated, with outbound network access blocked by default. That block should be enforced at the network level, not through instructions to the model. A run should stop automatically if an agent contacts outside systems, or finds or uses credentials that belong to someone else. If an agent reaches a real system, the affected organization and CERT-In should be told promptly. Earlier Disclosures by OpenAI and Anthropic OpenAI and Anthropic have both disclosed similar incidents this year. CERT-In did not say whether models from either company were involved in the Indian cases. In July, OpenAI disclosed that its models had compromised Hugging Face's platform. It is reviewing what its models did on the internet during training and testing, and notifying third parties whose security controls its models may have bypassed. In response to that disclosure, Anthropic began reviewing its own cyber evaluations. It has since reported 4 incidents in which Claude models gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems during evaluations built by the same outside partner. It has notified all affected parties. Of the 3 organizations in Anthropic's July disclosure, the 2 it reached had not detected the activity.

sgo2xe.text: A suspected advanced threat actor has been observed exploiting a security flaw in Fortinet FortiOS to deliver a previously unreported memory-resident ARM64 malware known as PEERSTITCH. The attack involves the exploitation of CVE-2025-61624 (CVSS score: 5.4), a path traversal flaw in the command line interpreter of FortiOS, FortiPAM, FortiProxy, and FortiSwitchManager that could allow a privileged attacker to achieve arbitrary write or delete files via specifically crafted arguments to existing commands. It was patched by Fortinet in April 2026. "PEERSTITCH leaves no persistent binary on disk, opens no listening ports and initiates no outbound network connections," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 researchers Daniel Gott and Shawn Westfall said. "Instead, it communicates through traffic generated by legitimate processes on the infected host, which makes the malware resistant to conventional endpoint and network detection." The cybersecurity company said it discovered the activity as part of its prolonged network intrusion against a telecommunications managed service provider that took place in September 2024. The multi-stage network intrusion is being tracked as CL-STA-0954 (aka UNC5820), with initial access obtained by exploiting a critical Fortinet FortiManager flaw dubbed FortiJump (CVE-2024-47575). Following a successful compromise of the appliance, the attackers are said to have exfiltrated an archive containing running configurations, cryptographic material, and database files containing information about more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls. Some of the harvested details are listed below - The FortiManager appliance's own serial number and its management relationships to every enrolled device Running configuration files for more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls across internal infrastructure and client networks Central management SQLite databases An inventory listing more than 500 FortiGate serial numbers alongside their respective public IP addresses Internal network topology maps, routing tables and interface configurations Ciphertext administrative, local, and SSL/VPN credentials Encoded cryptographic trust material, including public certificates, and private keys The stolen information was then used to conduct network reconnaissance, establish long-term access, intercept network traffic, set up unauthorized FortiGate SSL/VPN sessions to perimeter firewalls, deploy backdoors, and exploit a separate privilege-escalation vulnerability (i.e., CVE-2025-61624) to deploy PEERSTITCH. The malware is a 64-bit Linux ARM64 executable written in C. It includes an auto-script designed to download five components from an external server ("23.240.77[.]233:8085") - pM.js, an environment preparation script (self-deleting) a.js (saved as index.js), an Emscripten JavaScript runtime module a.wasm (saved as index.wasm), a compiled WebAssembly binary module b.js (saved as ipssem.js), a deployment orchestrator script dd (saved as lldprx), a native ARM64 ELF binary injector (PEERSTITCH core) The main phase of the attack begins after an execution delay. The orchestrator ("ipssem.js") launches "lldprx," which then serves as a process memory patching injector targeting two core FortiOS daemons: "/bin/miglogd" and "/bin/iked." Specifically, it locates the running processes associated with the two daemons, enumerates their memory layout, attaches to them using ptrace and halts their execution using PTRACE_INTERRUPT, allocates executable memory and writes malicious code into it, and redirects execution through the injected code. The end goal behind this hooking step is to create a "covert, memory-resident communication bridge" between the two legitimate FortiOS processes instead of using a conventional network connection or file, and use them as a cover to sidestep detection. Specifically, the miglogd hook is equipped to recognize a marker in the data it is passing through the process. This includes two specific markers - TCP port marker - 8550 (embedded within traffic data, not a listening port) IP address marker - 169.254.0.1 (link-local identifier used for pattern matching) Once this pattern is identified, it passes the associated session token or identifier to the iked daemon, whose hook later looks for that identifier while handling subsequent VPN sessions. If such a tag exists within that VPN session's injection buffer, it takes an alternative execution path, bypassing default FortiOS security validations. Put differently, the hooks injected into the two FortiOS processes change how the VPN daemon handles particular sessions. Besides deploying PEERSTITCH, the attackers have been observed establishing a separate command-and-control (C2) channel by leveraging the native Apache "mod_md" module on FortiGate firewalls in order to spawn an SSH-based reverse shell. "The attackers also impersonated the FortiManager platform to pull from managed firewalls of other hosts in the targeted network," the researchers said. "The attackers demonstrated proficiency in Fortinet appliance architecture, FortiOS internals and FortiOS management protocols." Although not definitive, it's suspected that the attackers may have exploited other flaws like CVE-2024-26009 and CVE-2024-26008 to carry out this task. However, Unit 42 emphasized that exploiting these vulnerabilities requires the device to be enrolled in FortiGate Cloud/FortiCloud SSO, which none of the affected firewalls held. In addition, CL-STA-0954 has been identified as undertaking various measures to remove forensic artifacts through termination of syslog generation, crash log clearing, logging telemetry disruption, and automatic deletion of rogue administrator accounts and auto-script objects after execution. "This intrusion highlights a growing threat, the weaponization of centralized edge management ecosystems to compromise downstream networks," Unit 42 said. "The discovery of the PEERSTITCH implant demonstrates the increasing technical maturity of edge-device malware." "By operating as a one-shot injector, avoiding persistent disk artifacts and building a covert inter-process communication bridge inside process memory, the attackers achieved sustained persistence while evading traditional monitoring."

16st4el.text: A newly disclosed critical flaw in the Linux kernel allows code inside a virtual machine to read memory on the host computer it runs on. A researcher demonstrated the leak against Vercel's live cloud sandboxes, and Vercel confirmed it. The flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-99999 and nicknamed PwnEscape, is in the Linux kernel's networking code, not in any one cloud's setup, so it reaches the shared layer that cloud providers use to keep customers' workloads apart. It was found in a Vercel security challenge and reported privately before any public release, and there is no sign it has been used in a real attack. What the Researcher Showed Paulos Yibelo of the security firm pwn.ai found that specially made network packets sent from inside a virtual machine could do three things, he explained in a technical write-up: read the host's memory, crash the host, and run code on it. All three come from the same kernel flaw. Vercel said in its report on the challenge that the memory leak was demonstrated against its production sandboxes. Each packet the guest sent out could carry back about 32 bytes of the host's memory, and the guest could keep going as long as it kept sending packets. The crash and code execution were observed only on the researcher's own machines, which were set up to match Vercel's. Two specially crafted packets were enough to crash a host and take down every sandbox running on it. Using the same flaw, the researcher then reached administrator control of a host, breaking out of the virtual machine. He stressed this was a lab result, "not a claim of root command execution in any vendor's production environment." "Our research ran through Omega-Pwn, an internal harness combining our own security research tooling with elements of SingularityNET's OmegaClaw architecture. It let us carry hypotheses, code traces, failed attempts, and experimental results across long-running research sessions. GPT-5.6 Sol was the primary reasoning engine. We directed the investigation, challenged its findings, and validated the interesting ones against actual kernel behavior on systems we controlled," Paulos Yibelo told The Hacker News. Vercel said no report in the challenge showed anyone reading a customer's files, secrets, or application data. How Severe It Is, and Who Can Set It Off The kernel's maintainers assigned the flaw CVE-2026-99999 and, in the published record, rated it 9.3 out of 10, or Critical. The U.S. National Vulnerability Database had received that entry but had not yet finished its own review. The same record lists the attack vector as local. In plain terms, the attacker has to already be running code inside a guest, as the researcher was. This is not a flaw that an outsider can exploit by sending packets across the open internet. It is not in CISA's catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities, and no real-world use has been reported. Why It Reaches Beyond Vercel Vercel Sandbox runs each customer's code in its own Firecracker microVM, a small virtual machine with its own copy of the Linux kernel, on bare-metal Amazon EC2 hosts. That microVM is the wall between one customer and the host, and between one customer and another. The flaw is not in that wall. It is in the Linux kernel's networking code, which the host runs. pwn.ai said Vercel's sandbox was already hardened beyond normal industry standards, with no misconfiguration it could find. Because almost every large cloud separates customer workloads on the same layer of the Linux kernel, Vercel said that a flaw there poses a risk to shared infrastructure rather than to any one provider. The Fix and the Fixed Versions The fix is a single Linux kernel change, commit 6785011f8b16, written by Red Hat's Michael S. Tsirkin and merged into the mainline kernel. It adds a check that a packet's checksum data cannot point into the IPv4 header before the kernel acts on it, and applies that check at five places in the networking code. The change is deliberately partial. Its author calls it "a defence in depth measure" and notes that a fuller check on the way packets enter the kernel still needs work. The maintainers backported the fix to the stable kernel branches. According to the CVE record, these are the first fixed versions in each supported branch: Stable branch First fixed version 5.10 5.10.272 5.15 5.15.223 6.1 6.1.190 6.6 6.6.159 6.12 6.12.113 6.18 6.18.57 7.2 7.2.11 Linux distributions ship their own kernels and often add this kind of fix without changing the version number, so check your distribution's advisory and whether the fix is in the kernel the host is actually running, not only the number from uname. What to Do Update the host kernel to one of the fixed versions above, or to the vendor build that includes the fix, and reboot into it. Updating only a guest's kernel does not fix the host. The sources give no separate workaround for this flaw if you cannot update yet. Where patching has to wait, the usual step is to limit what a break-in could reach. Vercel said it keeps host kernels up to date, disables nested virtualization, and runs each microVM under Firecracker's jailer, which grants the microVM process only the permissions it needs. That does not fix the flaw, but it narrows what an attacker who used it could do. Found in a $1 Million Challenge The flaw was found in a two-week challenge Vercel ran in August that offered up to $1 million in total to anyone who could break out of its sandbox. No single payout reached that figure. The top reward per report was $50,000; Vercel paid $242,000 across 1,285 reports, and this flaw was the one Critical finding. pwn.ai said it found the flaw in three days using its own AI-assisted research system, with the model doing the source-code analysis and human researchers directing the work. The firm put the cost at under $700 in API tokens. It was the latest case of researchers using a large language model to help find and chain real flaws, after a separate team used one earlier this year to reach internal systems at OpenAI.

j7vsws.text: Someone built a tool to steal data, then decided it should scare the victim for fun. Yes, that’s an actual feature. And somehow, it fits right in with this week's security stories.The rest gets interesting in different ways. A small permission can lead to a big theft. A trusted login can hide the wrong person. Old bugs are finding new victims, familiar tools are being put to strange uses, and some flaws are so simple you wonder how nobody spotted them sooner.There's a lot more hiding in the details, including a few twists you probably wouldn't expect. Here's what made the list this week.The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. Active ransomware exploitation Qilin and Settra ransomware groups are actively exploiting CVE-2026-0257, an authentication bypass vulnerability in PAN-OS GlobalProtect and Prisma Access. The vulnerability, disclosed in May 2026, has since come under active exploitation. "Because this access originates through an organization’s own VPN, malicious activity can resemble legitimate remote work and may go undetected until credential theft, lateral movement, data theft, or ransomware deployment is underway," ReliaQuest said. "Organizations should immediately upgrade affected deployments, disable authentication override cookies where they are not required, terminate all active GlobalProtect sessions after patching, and investigate unexpected connections, including sessions using hostnames such as 'kali.' Patching alone may not remove access established before remediation." Hybrid warfare escalates across Europe Russia is assessed to have escalated its use of hybrid, asymmetric warfare across Europe following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. "They do not involve troops moving across a country’s border or a state’s military dropping bombs on an adversary’s capital city," Recorded Future said. "Instead, they are a complex kit of psychological, cyber, and physical tactics meant to achieve several key aims: (1) Test the enemy’s defensive capabilities, as Russia evaluates whether to escalate aggression into a formal, kinetic conflict, (2) Degrade the enemy’s critical infrastructure, and (3) Sow an environment of fear in the enemy’s government and population to degrade the enemy’s ability to respond." DNS-powered wallet theft Infoblox has analyzed a cryptocurrency wallet-drainer kit, self-branded as Noir, that makes use of DNS TXT records to locate its hosted pool, which currently runs on Cloudflare Pages. It's delivered by means of a loader that queries the TXT record through public DoH services to learn which backend pool is active. "The drainer does not need a seed phrase, password, or private key," Infoblox said. "It tailors content to the user after receiving initial read permissions, developing a plan for the specific wallet. Then it obtains spending permissions that can look less alarming than a direct transfer and performs the theft from attacker-controlled infrastructure." It's suspected that the malware was created and maintained with AI assistance. Discord-based remote access threat A Rust-based remote access trojan dubbed CikaBika Bot has been observed being delivered via a document-themed lure containing a malicious LNK file and a PDF with an embedded payload. "The malware uses a Nim loader, PowerShell UAC bypass, and DLL search-order hijacking before leveraging Discord for C2, reconnaissance, remote execution, and data exfiltration through ngrok in observed malicious activity," Darktrace said. The malware also supports screenshot capture and file transfers. RAT combines theft and intimidation A Windows remote access trojan (RAT) called KGB RAT is being marketed on underground forums since late 2025 as being fully undetectable. It features a built-in crypter, HVNC, credential theft, ransomware, and an unusual set of psychological harassment capabilities, per Group-IB. "KGB RAT is, in practice, a full-featured malware package that gives attackers silent and persistent control over infected Windows machines," it said. "What sets it apart from comparable RAT families is not only its technical breadth — combining credential theft, keylogging, hidden desktop takeover, and ransomware in a single builder — but also a dedicated set of psychological harassment features, including screamer functions, jump scares, and forced blue screens of death. These 'fun settings,' as the developers themselves describe them, signal a threat actor profile comfortable weaponizing victim anxiety alongside data theft." A public disclosure referencing a KGB RAT server at version 0.1 dates to late January 2022, indicating the developer had been building and testing the malware for years before bringing it to market. Stealthy live-screen surveillance A multi-stage infection chain on Windows has been observed deriving a previously undocumented .NET RAT with live screen surveillance capability. It's been codenamed BotHelper RAT. "The first stage is a native x64 stager that fingerprints the host computer name, logged-on user, processor configuration, and installed memory, then connects to easyllms.xyz over HTTPS and retrieves a file named payload.bin from a path guarded by a long hexadecimal identifier, disabling TLS certificate validation beforehand," Point Wild said. "The second stage is BotHelper RAT. It copies itself to a hidden location, registers a scheduled task to relaunch every 30 minutes, patches the Antimalware Scan Interface, and registers with the same host that delivered it before polling a set of PHP endpoints for tasking." New Android anti-scam defenses Google said it's rolling out multi-layered protections across Google Messages and third-party messaging apps to protect Android users against mobile scams. This includes enhanced Scam Detection with Private AI Compute, link safety checks with Gemini Nano, and redesigned warnings before tapping unfamiliar links. Google also said it's bringing Scam Detection in chat notifications to warn users about suspicious messages directly from their notification shade to other Android devices in partnership with device makers. Other security improvements include automatic screen-share privacy to hide sensitive information in native apps, Chrome, and Android WebView, blocking apps from quietly enabling call forwarding in the background, and real-time verification for bank calls in collaboration with Banco do Brasil, Itaú Unibanco, and other leading banks. "Android checks incoming calls in real time to verify whether the bank actually initiated the call," Google said. "If an incoming caller claiming to represent a bank fails this verification check, Android hangs up the call and immediately alerts you." Since launching this feature in June 2026, Android has blocked more than 3 million spoofed calls from Banco do Brasil and Itaú Unibanco alone. AI model theft defenses strengthened Anthropic has disclosed that new measures like preserved thinking, two-stage classifiers, and charging for requests that are blocked by our safeguards before Claude responds in its Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 models have reduced data harvesting through distillation attacks by about 90% to 99%. Enterprise browser security controls Mozilla has launched Firefox Enterprise, a browser iteration "built for organizations with strict security, governance, and compliance requirements." Mozilla added, "IT and security teams get more control over their data, IT infrastructure and browser environment — helping strengthen technological independence and operational resilience." Self-healing WordPress backdoor Wordfence has detailed an unusual malware that's installed as a must-use WordPress plugin and makes use of "several self-healing mechanisms in place in order to survive removal. It also makes use of EtherHiding, a technique that hides the location of the attacker's servers behind a smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain, making the command channel resilient to takedown." The malware is capable of establishing administrator access, hiding the rogue administrator account, harvesting administrator passwords, remote site modification, data exfiltration, and spreading to other WordPress installations on the file system. Stolen credentials expose GitHub data Meta said it's notifying about 1,500 people, most of them its own employees in the U.S., after unknown threat actors broke into some of the company's GitHub repositories. The intrusion, detected a few weeks ago, involved the use of an employee's stolen credentials. The access has since been shut down, according to SecurityWeek. XWorm expands surveillance capabilities The malware known as XWorm has transitioned from an infostealer to a full-blown surveillance platform. The malware's plugin count has expanded from 35 to 46. The latest versions detected since July 2025 are V6.4, V6.5 "XWorm Reborn," V7.2, and V7.4. "The Maps plugin provides victims' GPS location without triggering a user prompt," Netskope said. "The Microphone plugin streams live audio from the victim’s device. HBrowser gives operators interactive control of authenticated browser sessions without touching credentials, bypassing MFA entirely. Webcam capture is also available on demand." Higher rewards for memory-safety bugs Google has announced that it's raising bug bounty rewards for some Chrome vulnerabilities, with a focus on memory safety issues. While the company lowered standard payout amounts for some vulnerabilities in April, such as a base reward of $500 for memory safety issues, it has now quadrupled base rates for memory safety flaws to $2,000. Vulnerabilities in Chrome's browser, GPU, and network processes can now earn researchers up to $20,000. Post-quantum readiness warning Microsoft is urging organizations to prepare their certificate systems for post-quantum authentication, stating that public key infrastructure (PKI), hardware security modules (HSMs), and security appliances need testing before deployment. "Organizations should begin now by inventorying certificate dependencies, assessing vendor roadmaps, identifying long-lived infrastructure, and creating non-production test environments," Microsoft said. "Early testing can surface compatibility and process gaps before post-quantum authentication is required at scale." AI tool credentials at risk A new malware-as-a-service (MaaS) infostealer written in Rust comes with its own loader and a built-in cryptocurrency clipper. "Warden Stealer is one of the first infostealers targeting configuration files and local data belonging to AI assistants and agentic coding tools," Gen Digital said. "Its builds are heavily obfuscated, morphed, and regularly updated to evade detection." Advanced browser data theft Newer versions of CastleStealer can "bypass app-bound encryption in Chromium-based browsers, execute commands remotely, and exfiltrate stolen information in small encrypted transmissions rather than a single large archive," according to Flashpoint. The C#-based stealer was first discovered in April 2026. AI developer credentials targeted The infostealer known as Aoki (aka Aokigahara) is targeting credential and session files used by AI coding assistants, including Claude, OpenAI's Codex, Cursor, Codeium, and Gemini. The stealer was first seen earlier this year. "API keys and Open Authorization (OAuth) or session tokens allow malicious activity to be carried out under a legitimate developer's identity and API quota," the Symantec Threat Hunter team said. "They can also expose connected repositories, cloud services and CI/CD pipelines linked to that account, and may bypass safeguards that assume requests originate from a trusted user." In a report published last month, Google-owned Wiz said AI service provider API keys are a hot commodity. "These AI credentials are highly lucrative; allowing attackers to freely run their own workloads or resell the access as part of the illicit LLM resale market," it said. "In addition, these keys can potentially grant access to historical chat logs that may contain sensitive corporate data, but we’re not aware of public occurrences of this scenario." Customizable MaaS infostealer K7 Labs has detailed a Python-based builder that is sold under a MaaS model and is used to embed an infostealer payload. "Rather than operating as a standalone stealer script, the builder follows a MaaS-style model," it said. "It allows operators to generate customized Windows executables using Nuitka or PyInstaller, with webhook configuration integrated into the build process." The stealer capabilities include anti-analysis techniques, persistence, credential harvesting, and data exfiltration. Cloud credential theft risk An SSRF vulnerability (GHSA-2phj-cp9f-qq6w, CVSS score: 8.5) in Harbor, the CNCF open-source container registry, can be abused by a registered user to steal cloud credentials. "Any registered user who can create a project can point a webhook at the cloud metadata endpoint and walk away with the server’s IAM credentials," OX Security said. Unauthenticated RCE chain A set of high-impact vulnerabilities in Adobe Experience Manager (AEM) can be abused to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). The chain combines four flaws: Unauthenticated DAM bulk import, stored cross-site scripting (XSS), unsafe XML parsing, and Groovy execution via /bin/asynccommand. The flaws affect only the cloud version of AEM and have been patched. Critical unauthenticated RCE Samsung has patched a critical security flaw (CVE-2026-110392, CVSS score: 9.8) in QA-Board that allows unauthenticated RCE. Samsung's QA-Board is an experiment-tracking tool that's used to organize, visualize, compare, and share research runs, specifically for algorithm and performance tuning. The problem stems from a case of improper neutralization of user-controlled data that could result in shell command injection. The vulnerability was flagged by Claude Opus 5.5. Linux root and container escape Security researcher Ziyi Guo has disclosed details of a critical Linux security vulnerability in NVIDIA's GPU Display Driver for Linux (CVE-2026-47595, CVSS score: 7.5, aka Bad UVM) that could allow an unprivileged user can write to read-only memory by taking advantage of the fact that the memory's permissions are not preserved. The vulnerability could be exploited to achieve code execution, escalation of privileges, denial-of-service, information disclosure, data tampering, and even a container escape. "By injecting our exploit code into nvidia-persistenced, we first force the hijacked process to execute a UVM-based local privilege escalation (LPE)," the researcher said. "Once the privilege barrier is crossed, we trigger the subsequent operations, ultimately granting us the ability to execute commands on the host with full root access." Active command injection attacks A command injection vulnerability in EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition (CVE-2026-106931, CVSS score: 8.5) has come under active exploitation in the wild. The flaw affects customers using version 2.20 or later with statistics enabled, which is turned on by default. Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary OS commands with root or SYSTEM privileges on affected systems. It's currently not known how the flaw is being exploited, by whom, and who is being targeted. Critical unpatched SQL injection Rapid7 has disclosed details of a critical SQL Injection vulnerability in Channel Software WebAlliance eCommerce (CVE-2026-108065, CVSS score: 9.8). "The exploit allows a malicious actor to read sensitive data from the database, or, if the database user has high privileges, run system commands on the database server," Rapid7 said. "The SQL Injection exploit can be leveraged to view sensitive information in the database, such as user PII and passwords. If logged in with DB admin privileges, the vulnerability can be exploited to run system commands on the server running the database." Four code execution flaws patched NSD has released patches for four security flaws (CVE-2026-101341, CVE-2026-101339, CVE-2026-101338, and CVE-2026-101337) that could be exploited to achieve execution of arbitrary commands. The vulnerabilities, credited to Qifan Zhang from Palo Alto Networks and Gaurang Maheta, have been patched in NSD 4.15.3 or newer. Potential VM-to-host escape The Xen project has published details of CVE-2026-79610, a race condition in Xen's grant-table mechanism that could be abused to compromise the security of a virtual machine host and allow an unprivileged guest to elevate its privileges to that of the host. All Xen versions from 4.0 onwards are vulnerable. The issue has been addressed in xsa517.patch. As mitigation, it's advised to use the "gnttab=max-ver:1" hypervisor command line option or the "max_grant_version=1" guest configuration option for guests. The project maintainers credited Anthropic's Claude Opus with the discovery and Teddy Astie of Vates for diagnosing it as a security issue. SYSTEM-level remote code execution A Windows security vulnerability in MyReport Updater 2.1.1 can permit an attacker to seize control of a machine, including remotely, without authentication. "An attacker with standard user privileges can set an arbitrary reference server," Quarkslab said. "If MyReportUpdaterService can contact this server over gRPC on TCP port 9095, the attacker can write files into a chosen directory with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges. The attacker can use this file-write access to place a DLL that will be loaded by a privileged process. The DLL code is then executed with high privileges. This vulnerability gives full control of the Citrix server. It can also affect other machines where the vulnerable MyReport solution is installed." If there's one thing this week's stories make clear, it's that attackers don't always need a clever trick. Sometimes a stolen login, a forgotten setting, or one small mistake is enough. And even when the bug gets fixed, the trouble it caused might still be sitting there.The lesson is pretty simple: don't just check what's broken. Check who got in, what they touched, and whether they can come back. Keep an eye on the things everyone assumes are safe. Those are often the ones nobody looks at until something goes wrong. That's it for this edition. See you next week, hopefully with fewer surprises.

1jd6law.text: Candiru, an Israeli maker of spyware sold to governments, infected devices at the news network Al Jazeera through ordinary online ads, in attacks that needed no click or other action from the user, researchers at the Citizen Lab said Thursday. The hidden attack code ran the moment an ad loaded on the screen, and in some cases the ad loaded out of sight, in the background. The Citizen Lab, a research group at the University of Toronto, said this is the first public, technical confirmation that mercenary spyware, meaning hacking tools sold to governments, has reached real devices through targeted ads. The method had been described before from leaked company documents, but not shown in a live attack. The researchers recovered the spyware itself from one device, but not the exploit that breaks into the browser or app to install it. That first break-in step is described from how the attack was set up, not from captured code. How the Attack Worked The ads were placed by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a normal digital advertising firm. Each ad carried a small piece of code that, when the ad loaded, quietly sent the device's advertising ID and internet address back to a Discover-Tech server, the researchers found. That server decided whether the device belonged to a target. If it did, the server sent back attack code for the browser or app to run. If it did not, the server sent nothing. Because the ad itself carried no attack code, the ad networks that delivered it had nothing harmful to detect. At Al Jazeera, at least 45 devices were targeted in 2024 and 2025, the Citizen Lab said, and it linked the attacks to Candiru with high confidence. The researchers did not say which government was behind the operation. The network gave the researchers its traffic logs. On infected devices, the logs showed the same order each time: first contact with a Discover-Tech ad server, then a Candiru server that screens the device, then a command-and-control server that runs the spyware. Al Jazeera also pulled one Windows program file off a compromised device. Its code used the same distinctive techniques as a Candiru tool the Citizen Lab took apart in 2021, which is the basis for the high-confidence link. Al Jazeera staff were targeted once before. In 2020, dozens of its journalists' iPhones were hacked with NSO Group's Pegasus spyware, in a different operation that used a different method. Who Discover-Tech and Candiru Are Google and the advertising trade group IAB Europe had both listed Discover-Tech as an approved ad vendor from 2020 until this month. The company was registered in Israel in 2020 and is led by its chief executive, Dekel Boni. Candiru is one of the better-known names in the spyware trade. The United States put it on a trade blacklist in 2021 over spyware used to target government officials, journalists, and activists. In 2025, its assets were bought by a U.S. investment firm, Integrity Partners, and moved into a new company, reported to be Integrity Labs, that the sanctions do not cover. What the Platforms Did After the researchers shared their findings, Google and IAB Europe removed Discover-Tech from their vendor lists in early October, the Citizen Lab said. Google cut off the company's access to its ad exchanges, Beeswax removed it, Vungle paused its access for a review, and Eskimi blocked its accounts. Google told Reuters it had worked with the researchers and removed Discover-Tech "for systematically violating our policies." IAB Europe said it suspended the company after an audit found policy violations. Comcast, which owns Beeswax, said it acted "following recent activity." Discover-Tech, Candiru's owners, Al Jazeera, and the Russian ad network Yandex did not respond to Reuters. Discover-Tech's website was still online on Thursday and said nothing about the findings. How Far the Ads Reached Discover-Tech's reach went far beyond Al Jazeera. On one of its platforms, the company placed nearly four billion ad bids between March and June 2026, the Citizen Lab said, and the ads carrying the hidden callback code appeared in about 75,000 phone apps and 120,000 websites. Confiant, a U.S. ad-security firm that investigated alongside the Citizen Lab, put Discover-Tech's traffic at roughly 10 million ads a day. The ads turned up on the networks of governments and large institutions, the Citizen Lab said, including NATO, the United Nations, European Union bodies, government offices in about two dozen countries, chipmakers, and news organizations. An ad appearing on a network is not proof that anyone there was infected. It shows only how widely the system could reach. Confiant found that the small number of ads it could tie directly to Candiru were low-volume and mostly reached home and mobile internet connections, rather than the sensitive networks themselves. What Defenders Can Check Both groups published the web addresses and files associated with the operation, so defenders can block them and search their own records. Organizations whose staff may have seen the ads, especially on the networks named in the report, can look for the attack's order of connections: a device reaching a Discover-Tech ad server, then a Candiru screening server, then a command-and-control server. Among the published indicators: SHA-256 (recovered spyware sample): 255869de85e2a171993fc5eb8a556d873a1b8966e040f6f55926f2fa2d595cc8 Domain (Discover-Tech ad server): mtrtb[.]com Full list: the indicators in Confiant's report, including the command-and-control servers. Security researchers have warned for years that the ad-buying system could be turned to this use. In December, leaked documents tied the spyware maker Intellexa to a similar ad-based tool called Aladdin, though no live infection through it had been shown.

1sk9stz.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 15, 2026Cyber Espionage / Malware The threat actor known as Silent Lynx has been attributed to a fresh set of attacks targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). The activity, observed from June 2025 through August 2026, involves four different infection chains that make use of macro-enabled documents, PS2EXE downloaders, GitHub-hosted PowerShell, and crafted WinRAR archives exploiting CVE-2025-8088. The attacks lead to the deployment of custom reverse shells like FoalShell, Chvost, Laplas, and PickleShell that facilitate interactive remote access to compromised hosts, according to Cisco Talos and Recorded Future Insikt Group, which are tracking the campaign under the monikers UAT-6275 and TAG-193. "UAT-6275's targeting is concentrated in Central Asia, and the wider CIS region," security researcher Ashley Shen said. "Across the reviewed campaigns, observed victims and lure themes span nine countries: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia, and Belarus." Silent Lynx was first publicly documented by Seqrite Labs in early 2025, highlighting the threat actor's attacks on embassies, lawyers, government-backed banks, and think tanks across Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan. It's assessed to be a Kazakhstan-nexus threat actor active since at least 2020, sharing overlaps with other clusters codenamed YoroTrooper (aka Comrade Saiga, ShadowSilk, and SturgeonPhisher), ShadowSilk, Cavalry Werewolf, and Tomiris. It's suspected that both UAT-6275 and YoroTrooper are part of the same broader activity cluster, although no direct indicator or toolset overlap has been observed between the two. Earlier this year, VMRay disclosed that a threat cluster it tracks as Hydra Saiga compromised at least 34 organizations across 8 countries since December 2024, with reconnaissance efforts extending to over 200 additional targets across the world. It's worth noting that both Comrade Saiga and Hydra Saiga refer to the same threat actor. The "hydra" prefix in the tracking alias is a reference to the adversary's heavy focus on breaching infrastructure linked specifically to water resources in Central Asia using a mix of custom implants written in Rust, Go, and Python and Living-off-the-Land techniques. Attack chains mounted by the threat actor involve the use of spear-phishing emails containing diplomatic relations, international trade, energy, and aviation-themed decoy documents. No less than eight campaigns have been identified across the region between January 2025 and May 2026. The phishing emails are sent from compromised government accounts and make use of official-looking documents to lend the social engineering attack a veneer of credibility. "Identified lures included a diplomatic letter addressed to Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a Turkmenistan airspace application form, and a business proposal concerning Russia’s Orsk Oil Refinery," Recorded Future said. What's more, three publicly accessible staging directories linked to the threat actor have been found to host Linux-compatible tooling and a publicly available proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2025-25257, an SQL injection flaw in Fortinet FortiWeb, suggesting a possible expansion of the threat actor's operational capabilities. Infection sequences have been found to employ four different pathways - June 2025 - Using macro-enabled Word documents to download and run a second-stage binary. July 2025 - Using downloaders built with PS2EXE, a tool that packages PowerShell scripts as Windows executables, to fetch reverse-shell payloads and create scheduled tasks for persistence. October 2025 - Using a malicious shortcut (LNK) within a RAR archive to launch PowerShell responsible for retrieving and executing a GitHub-hosted script that provides remote shell access. Subsequent iterations also download PickleShell and stage it in the Windows Startup folder so that it's automatically launched every time a user logs in to the system. April 2026 - Using a RAR archive that exploits a WinRAR flaw (CVE-2025-8088) to drop PickleShell in the Windows Startup folder.
