Weil$19,000,000Confirmed attack; ransom payment unverified. White & Case$30,000,000Not provided WilmerHale$17,000,000Confirmed May 2026 data breach. Total Reported$206,950,000 Silent Ransom Group, also tracked as Luna Moth and UNC3753, emerged after Conti shut down in 2022. Despite its ransomware label, it does not need to lock files. Operators trick employees into granting access, steal documents, and threaten to publish them. Law firms have been a major focus because they hold private client information. CybersecurityNews previously covered the group’s IT support impersonation attacks against law firms. Attackers call employees, pose as internal support staff, and persuade them to grant remote access. Legitimate software helps the activity blend into routine work, reducing reliance on malware that security tools might otherwise detect. Related reporting on Luna Moth’s fake helpdesk domains describes websites designed to resemble company support services. Once they gain access, tools such as WinSCP and Rclone can transfer stolen files. The pressure comes from the possible disclosure of confidential records, not a sudden loss of access to business systems. Crystal found instructions to use fresh wallets, keep victim funds separate, and avoid combining payouts. Operators sometimes broke those rules, linking transactions investigators could trace. Smaller payments also reached regulated exchanges, creating potential leads through customer identity records. The analysis describes cash conversion through instant exchangers, couriers, and a Bitcoin-to-Zelle service. For defenders, the attack chain makes identity checks essential. Employees should verify support requests through known internal channels before granting access. Organizations should restrict remote access, deploy phishing-resistant authentication, and train staff to recognize phone-based deception. Working systems don’t prove sensitive files stay safe. 1w6ljoy.text: A malicious Android PDF reader distributed through Google Play has recorded more than 10,000 installs while serving as an installer for the Anatsa banking trojan. The finding shows how a routine document tool can become a route for malware that puts banking passwords and financial accounts at risk. The installation figure describes the reach of the reader app, not a confirmed count of successful banking infections or stolen accounts. The available alert also does not identify affected banks, victim countries, financial losses, or whether Google has since removed this particular listing, wile those details remain unconfirmed. Researchers from Zscaler ThreatLabz identified the malicious installer and shared its indicators in an October 8 alert on X. They described the application as an Android PDF reader with over 10,000 installs and published separate file hashes for the installer and the Anatsa payload, alongside their command-and-control addresses. The discovery follows earlier cases involving similar disguises. In April, a fake document reader campaign used a different package to distribute Anatsa before Google removed that app. That earlier removal should not be confused with the status of the newly reported reader, which the current alert does not establish. Malicious PDF Reader With 10,000+ Installs Anatsa, also known as TeaBot, uses a dropper model: the app installed first acts as a delivery tool for a separate malicious component. This separation helps explain why a download that appears useful can later expose a phone to banking malware. The latest alert identifies both stages but does not provide a full execution trace. In its technical analysis of Anatsa, ThreatLabz documented earlier campaigns that downloaded additional code and presented the final payload as an app update. Some samples checked the device environment before proceeding, helping the malware avoid test systems used by researchers. These are documented family techniques, not confirmed findings for every new sample. ThreatLabz also documented malformed APK archive headers that made older payloads harder to inspect, along with encrypted code loaded at runtime. APK files are Android installation packages; hiding their contents can disrupt tools that inspect files without running them. The new alert does not confirm whether these samples use those methods. The broader use of Google Play stealth loaders shows why unexpected update requests deserve attention even when the original app came from an official store. A request to install an extra component outside the normal update process can move the user from a harmless-looking utility to the banking payload. ThreatLabz has uncovered another new Anatsa installer that is distributed via the Google Play Store. The application is disguised as an Android PDF reader that currently has over 10,000 installs. The IOCs for this campaign are listed below: Google Play Store URL… pic.twitter.com/duQA0myTAi — Zscaler ThreatLabz (@Threatlabz) October 8, 2026 For this campaign, ThreatLabz listed one installer-related command-and-control URL and two payload command-and-control endpoints. Keeping those roles separate matters during an investigation: the installer and the banking trojan are different files, and each has its own published MD5 hash. The alert does not explain the exact contents returned by the installer URL. Why Banking Accounts Are at Risk Earlier ThreatLabz research found that Anatsa requested SMS and accessibility permissions, contacted its control server, and checked for targeted financial apps. The server then supplied fake login pages matching apps on the phone. Credentials entered into those pages were sent to the attackers rather than the bank. A previous Anatsa document reader outbreak reached more than 100,000 downloads and used fake banking screens to capture account details. That history explains the concern around this new reader, but its target list and permission behavior still require sample-specific verification rather than assumptions based on older campaigns. What Android Users Should Do Users who installed the identified reader should remove it, review granted permissions, and scan their phones with a trusted security tool. Keep Google Play Protect enabled and question unexpected requests for SMS or accessibility access. If banking activity looks suspicious, contact the bank promptly and change account passwords from a trusted device. For security teams, the package name can support app inventory checks, while file hashes help match samples against the reported installer and payload. Network logs can be searched for the listed domain and IP endpoints. Matches should be reviewed in context to establish which device communicated, when contact occurred, and whether malware executed. lre2pv.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 20, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Cybercrime Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a ClickFix delivery platform called ROMULUS that's being used to distribute malware such as Legion Loader. According to Forescout Research - Vedere Labs, ROMULUS is akin to a malware delivery service that employs ClickFix-style lures on bogus landing pages to trick unsuspecting users into running malicious commands and infecting their own machines. "ROMULUS may be a privately operated panel, a commercial cybercriminal delivery service, an affiliate framework, or software that has been copied between operators," security researcher Sai Molige said in an analysis. The cybersecurity company said it identified six IP addresses running ROMULUS - 96.62.224[.]81 86.109.75[.]7 151.240.151[.]223 23.94.145[.]224 93.152.224[.]118 2.27.248[.]127 Notably, the IP address "96.62.224[.]81" was identified as hosting a ClickFix script and an MSI installer file in connection with another campaign that has been found to leverage malicious ChatGPT Custom GPTs to direct victims to a fake URL responsible for serving the ClickFix lure. Forescout's own analysis has since uncovered the same malware being delivered via another server, 86.109.75[.]7, that also hosted a panel codenamed ROMULUS. In addition, a separate chain triggered via ClickFix has been used to run a PowerShell script, which then delivers Legion Loader, a malware loader also called Satacom downloader, CurlyGate, and RobotDropper. As of writing, it's not known who is behind the ROMULUS platform. However, it shares no overlaps with RomulusLoader, a malware family associated with Silver Fox (aka TA4922), a China-aligned threat actor known for repeatedly using tax-related pretexts to distribute remote access trojans like ValleyRAT (aka Winos 4.0), DcRAT, and potentially Venom RAT via DLL sideloading techniques. The ROMULUS platform exposes two endpoints that are designed to download a PowerShell staging script, which decides the payload to be fetched next: a trojanized MSI installer carrying a malware loader or an encrypted archive containing Legion Loader that's inflated to nearly 1 GB with repetitive padding to bypass upload limits, sandbox budgets, or static-analysis thresholds. The loader, for its part, communicates with a remote server to fetch and run additional payloads. The findings indicate how ClickFix is evolving beyond a social engineering technique into a highly effective entry point for malware. To mitigate the threat, it's essential to hunt for suspicious PowerShell commands and DLL sideloading events.

1kvxe5v.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 20, 2026Vulnerability / Endpoint Security Siemens has addressed a DLL sideloading vulnerability impacting Siemens Software Center that it said has been exploited in ClickFix attacks. The high-severity vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-110936 (CVSS v4 score: 8.4), could allow an attacker to place a specially-crafted DLL in a directory the application searches, resulting in execution of malicious code with the same privileges as the affected service. "The affected application loads dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) from an uncontrolled search path," Siemens said in an advisory. "This could allow an authenticated local attacker to place a specially crafted DLL in a directory that the application searches, leading to arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the affected application." The issue has been patched in version 4.0.9.8. Huntress Labs researcher Jose Oregon has been credited with discovering and reporting the shortcoming. In a separate alert, Siemens said attackers have abused a genuine copy of Siemens Software Center with a valid signature and placed their own crafted DLL ("archive.dll") next to it to trigger the execution of malicious code. "They chose this program as a carrier because it is signed and trusted, and because version 3.5.8.7, the latest version at the time, loaded helper files from its own folder without checking them," Siemens added. Specifically, threat actors have been found leveraging "msiexec.exe" to launch "AllMyBasic.msi," which then executes "SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe." The activity has been attributed to a ClickFix delivery platform called Romulus, which was detailed by Forescout last week as being used to deliver Legion Loader and other malware using DLL sideloading. According to Huntress, some of these campaigns have leveraged malicious ChatGPT Custom GPTs to direct victims to a fake URL responsible for serving a ClickFix lure, which when copied and executed by the victim, runs PowerShell code to drop an MSI installer that abuses DLL sideloading to ultimately deploy a remote access trojan. Siemens has shared the following indicators of compromise - 96.62.218[.]59 (Payloading hosting and command-and-control) wizardexpensive[.]com (Payloading hosting and command-and-control) 2.27.248[.]127 (Distribution channel of AllMyBasic.msi) Besides updating Siemens Software Center to version 4.0.9.8 or later and starting the application to apply the update, organizations are advised to block the IP addresses and domains associated with the malicious activity and look for "SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe" running from "AppData\Local\Programs" and started by "msiexec.exe."

11e0hy4.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 20, 2026Cyber Espionage / Data Security A U.S. court on Monday granted the U.S. government's request to detain a former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a recording device in an executive conference room at the company's San Francisco office to allegedly steal sensitive secrets. In a new court filing Sunday, prosecutors revealed that Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, was "in frequent communications via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family" throughout 2025 and 2026. Alfozan is said to have communicated with the Saudi royal as recently as October 5, 2026, four days before he was arrested. "Among other things, the individual told the defendant that an artificial intelligence initiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and wanted the defendant to join it," the filing reads. "In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,' indicating he agreed." The Saudi Royal Family member is said to have repeatedly attempted to recruit Alfozan and even asked when he planned to leave OpenAI, to which the defendant said he wouldn't do so until his stock vested. Alfozan joined OpenAI as an engineer around July 2025 with an annual base salary of $385,000. Last week, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) revealed that he had been arrested for allegedly inserting a stealthy audio recording device into a USB port on the back of a television in the executive conference room to capture sensitive conversations. The defendant is also said to have modified the device to prevent data transfer between it and the television and encrypted the content stored on the device's microSD card. In addition, he used his wife's personal ChatGPT account to research how to "build a continuous audio recorder" to "captur[e] microphone audio and save compressed WAV recordings to an SD card." "In the days and weeks before placing the device, the defendant (i) used an OpenAI productivity agent to ascertain which 'meeting rooms' OpenAI 'leadership and exec[utives]' used, and where they met with 'external partners'; and (ii) spent considerable time near the conference room where he later installed the device," the filing said. Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison. Prosecutors also argued that Alfozan is a flight risk, stating he has "ample resources... and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government that has (i) no extradition treaty with the United States; (ii) limitless resources; and (iii) the ability to provide extraordinary travel assistance," according to the filing. Shortly after details of his arrest became public knowledge, it emerged that the defendant had planned to depart to Riyadh with his wife and son on a one-way ticket on October 12, 2026. Although he was arrested three days prior, his wife and son are said to have already left the U.S. without him. The day before her departure, Alfozan's wife allegedly told the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agents that her U.S. visa was expiring and that she, along with her son, were permanently shifting back to Saudi Arabia. "The defendant went to significant lengths to create customized, encrypted recording devices to secretly record highly sensitive meetings involving senior OpenAI personnel and executives, high-level business counterparts, and government officials, all while communicating with individuals of significance in Saudi Arabia and pursuing opportunities in – and making plans to travel to – Saudi Arabia," the filing said. Stating the U.S. government's investigation is ongoing, prosecutors said a search of the defendant's residence and a "preliminary review" of his electronic devices, including his cellphone, uncovered several pieces of evidence - Several electronic components similar to those in the customized devices the defendant installed in the OpenAI conference room and had in his missing bag were identified in his residence. Photographs from his iPhone dated between September 22 and 28, 2026, that depict one additional concealed recording device, as well as what appear to be the input/output panels on TVs and other electronic devices in various locations in OpenAI buildings, including a second conference room where sensitive meetings took place. A deleted note on his cellphone from September 2026 included links to various recording devices, including those made by Seeed Studio, the same manufacturer whose devices were found in OpenAI's offices and his residence. Browsing history showed that the defendant accessed a folder called "Saudi Gov Docs" on October 4, 2026, and he used an OpenAI productivity agent to inquire about various Saudi-related business and government-related engagements from the Saudi Ministry of Communication and Information Technology (MCIT) between July 6, 2026, and September 21, 2026. "The defendant leveraged his skills as a highly-educated engineer to create sophisticated recording devices that – the evidence strongly suggests – he intended to bring with him to Saudi Arabia," the filing said. "Whether the defendant wanted to record OpenAI meetings to enrich himself by enhancing his own business prospects, or to provide aid a foreign government, or both, his conduct is criminal and it presents a danger to innovation in the Silicon Valley and a concern for the national security of the United States."
